#### 10.39  Diffuse alveolar hemorrhage cause off DAH etiology table · pulmonary pathology

**Raw `Text` field:**

```
<u>Cocaine-induced lung toxicity</u> presents with rapid onset of <b>dyspnea</b>; diffuse, <b>bilateral lung opacities</b>; and <b>hypoxemia</b> that is a result of {{c1::diffuse alveolar hemorrhage}}
```

**Reads as →**

Cocaine-induced lung toxicity presents with rapid onset of dyspnea; diffuse, bilateral lung opacities; and hypoxemia that is a result of 【diffuse alveolar hemorrhage】

**`Extra` field →**

- When inhaled, cocaine undermines the blood-alveolar barrier via thermal damage (scorching hot smoke), ischemia-reperfusion injury (intense pulmonary vasospasm), and direct cellular toxicity

- This can result in diffuse alveolar hemorrhage, a form of widespread alveolar capillary bleeding

- AKA "crack lung"

| Diffuse Alveolar Hemorrhage |
| --- |
| Etiology & pathogenesis | Clinical presentation & diagnosis | Management |
| - Pulmonary capillaritis: ANCA vasculitis, SLE, antiphospholipid antibodies- Bland hemorrhage: mitral stenosis, anticoagulation- Alveolar damage: viral pneumonitis, ARDS, drug-induced (e.g., cocaine, amiodarone) | - Dyspnea, hypoxemia, hemoptysis (absent in ~50%) & blood loss anemia- CXR or CT: diffuse ground-glass opacities- Bronchoscopy: progressive blood on serial lavage | - Treat underlying cause- Supportive care: oxygen, mechanical ventilation; avoid anticoagulation |
| ANCA = antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody; ARDS = acute respiratory distress syndrome; CXR = chest x-ray; SLE = systemic lupus erythematosus |

## 11. Numeric Values, Cutoffs & Lab Values

This technique clozes a precise number together with the thing that makes it meaningful: its unit, its comparison operator, or the named quantity it represents. The fundamental move is to put the entire numeric expression inside one deletion so the learner must reproduce the value AND its unit, not just a bare digit. Write `{{c1::≥ 126 mg/dL}}`, not `≥ {{c1::126}} mg/dL` and not `{{c1::126}} {{c1::mg/dL}}`. A number with no unit ("126") is ambiguous and untestable; a number with the wrong unit is a clinical error, so the unit travels inside the cloze. Inequality symbols (≥, <, >) and ranges ("2 - 4 mm", "10-15%") likewise belong inside the deletion because they ARE the answer.

Use the `::hint` slot to remove ambiguity about what FORM the answer should take when the bare blank could be answered many ways. Classic hint patterns here: `{{c1::≥ 1 hour::Duration}}` (tells you a time is wanted), `{{c1::1 - 2 weeks::range}}` (signals a range, not a point value), `{{c1::25°C aka 77°F aka 298K::°C/°F/K}}` (asks for all three unit systems), and `{{c1::25%::%}}` (cues percent so you don't write a decimal). The hint is for disambiguation, not for giving the answer away  -  `::range` or `::Duration` narrows the expected format without leaking the number.

Frame the stem so the number is the single point of recall: "What is the diagnostic cutoff for fasting plasma glucose...?" → `{{c1::≥ 126 mg/dL}}`. Equalities and constants follow the same shape: `Avogadro's Number = {{c1::6.022 × 10^23 = 1 mol}}`. When a single statement contains several equivalent values (1 atm = 760 mmHg = 760 torr = 101.3 kPa), put each value in its own `c1` deletion so they test together as one card but each blank must be filled.

This differs from neighboring techniques: a plain term/definition cloze hides a word or concept, whereas here the load-bearing answer is quantitative. When a card mixes a name and a number ("Heart failure with LVEF < {{c1::30%}}"), the number is what this technique governs. Avoid over-clozing the surrounding prose  -  keep the deletion tight around the value and let the stem carry the context.

**Canonical syntax:** `{{c1::<number><unit-or-operator>::<format-hint>}}  -  keep the unit/operator inside the cloze; use ::hint only to signal the expected form (Duration, range, %, units).`

**When to use:** Use whenever the fact worth memorizing is a specific number: a diagnostic cutoff, lab threshold, dose, duration, percentage, constant, or physical/anatomical range. Reach for the ::hint slot when a bare blank wouldn't tell the learner what unit or form to supply.

**Watch out for:** Don't strand the unit outside the cloze (`{{c1::126}} mg/dL`) or split the value and unit into separate deletions  -  the answer must include the unit. Don't leak the number through an over-specific hint, and don't bury a single number inside a giant multi-clause deletion where the quantitative point gets lost.

**Best practices**

- Cloze the number WITH its unit as one unit: `{{c1::≥ 126 mg/dL}}`, never `≥ {{c1::126}} mg/dL`.
- Keep inequality symbols and ranges inside the deletion (`{{c1::< 30%}}`, `{{c1::2 - 4 mm}}`)  -  the operator is part of the answer.
- Add a `::hint` only to disambiguate the expected form (`::Duration`, `::range`, `::%`, `::°C/°F/K`), not to reveal the value.
- Write a stem that pins the number as the single recall target ('What is the diagnostic cutoff for...?').
- For equivalences, give each equal value its own same-numbered cloze (`{{c1::760 mmHg}} = {{c1::760 torr}} = {{c1::101.3 kPa}}`).
- Use a contrasting non-clozed fact in EXTRA (the other thresholds, the dark-adapted range) so the value is anchored without being given away on the front.
- Prefer self-contained statements; let context live in the stem so the blank tests only the quantity.

**Worked examples (70)**

#### 11.1  Bare percentage as the answer · physiology (calcium binding)

**Raw `Text` field:**

```
What percent of total <b>Ca<sup>2+</sup> </b>in the blood is <b>bound to plasma protein</b>?<br><br><div>{{c1::40%}} </div>
```

**Reads as →**

What percent of total Ca^(2+) in the blood is bound to plasma protein?

【40%】

**`Extra` field →**

Total calcium in the blood is distributed as follows:

- 40%: Bound to proteins (mainly albumin)

- 45%: Ionized (free and physiologically active)

- 10-15%: Complexed with anions (e.g., phosphate, sulfate, citrate)

- In conditions like hypoalbuminemia (e.g., liver cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome), total calcium levels may be low, even if ionized calcium levels remain normal

- Alkalosis increases calcium binding to albumin, which lowers ionized calcium levels

- Acidosis decreases calcium binding to albumin, which raises ionized calcium levels

> **Why it works:** Simplest form: a clean stem whose only blank is a percent value, showing the number itself is the recall target.

```

What is the estimated week of gestation if the measured fundal height is at the navel?

Fundal height ~ gestational age ± 3 weeks

**Raw `Text` field:**

```

```

**Reads as →**

Specific heat capacity is the amount of energy necessary to raise the temperature of one gram of substance by 【1° C or 1 K】.

**`Extra` field →**

Remember, temperature is average kinetic energy

 
 [image: cc83e87109cbe466ac5bc47c962ffe79.jpg]
Photo Credit: OpenStax, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
 
Specific Heat Capacity (lower case "c")

c = amount of energy needed to raise one gram of a specific substance by 1°C or 1K. 
Units: J/g·°C
Equation: \(Q =\) \(mc\Delta T\)

Heat Capacity (capital "C")
C = amount of heat required to raise the temperature of an entire object (regardless of mass) by 1°C or 1K. 
Units: J/°C
Equation: \(Q =\) \(C\Delta T\)

Khan Academy Link

> **Why it works:** The clozed value gives two equivalent unit expressions, teaching that equivalent forms can share one blank.

#### 11.42  ultrafilterable Ca2+ in blood = 60% · physiology

**Raw `Text` field:**

```
<div>What percent of total <b>Ca<sup>2+</sup> </b>in the blood is <b>ultrafilterable</b>?</div><br><div>{{c1::60%}}</div>
```

**Reads as →**

What percent of total Ca^(2+) in the blood is ultrafilterable?

【60%】

**`Extra` field →**

i.e., not bound to protein (albumin)

Total calcium in the blood is distributed as follows:

- 40%: Bound to proteins (mainly albumin)

- 45%: Ionized (free and physiologically active)

- 10-15%: Complexed with anions (e.g., phosphate, sulfate, citrate)

- In conditions like hypoalbuminemia (e.g., liver cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome), total calcium levels may be low, even if ionized calcium levels remain normal

- Alkalosis increases calcium binding to albumin, which lowers ionized calcium levels

- Acidosis decreases calcium binding to albumin, which raises ionized calcium levels

#### 11.56  wait 2 weeks after stopping MAOI before serotonergic drugs · pharm

**Raw `Text` field:**

```
<div>Patients must wait {{c1::2 weeks}} <i>after</i> <u>stopping MAO inhibitors</u> before <b>starting serotonergic drugs</b> and/or <b>stopping dietary restrictions</b><br></div>
```

**Reads as →**

Patients must wait 【2 weeks】 after stopping MAO inhibitors before starting serotonergic drugs and/or stopping dietary restrictions

**`Extra` field →**

- Reverse is also true (i.e., must wait 2 weeks after stopping SSRIs or other serotonergic drugs before starting MAO inhibitors, and fluoxetine requires 5 weeks due to its long half-life)

- Phenelzine irreversibly inhibits both MAO A and B, resulting in increased presynaptic concentration and release of MAO neurotransmitters

- It takes up to two weeks to regulate MAO synthesis to appropriate levels for normal degradation, avoiding the risk of SSRI-induced serotonin syndrome

 [image: 9f834f7af8b40e27ceed6269cc1fa455.webp]

> **Why it works:** Drug-safety interval clozed inline; extra adds the 5-week fluoxetine exception.

-_( )【c1: Decreased】 PaCO_(2)

**`One by one` field →** y

## 12. Direction-of-Change (↑ / ↓) Cards

Direction-of-change cards test whether a value goes UP, DOWN, or stays the SAME in response to some cause. The key move is to cloze the DIRECTION, not the analyte. The analyte (TSH, calcium, GFR, V_max...) stays visible in the prompt as the thing being asked about, and the hidden answer is just "Increased" / "Decreased" / "Unchanged" (or the arrows ↑ / ↓ / normal). This forces the learner to commit to a directional prediction rather than recognizing a noun.

The simplest form is a question stem plus a one-word reveal: `What is the effect of <cause> on <analyte>? {{c1::Increased}}`. Because the answer is binary-ish, a symbol-legend hint is enormously valuable: `{{c1::Decreased::↑ / ↓ / Normal}}` or `{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}}`. The hint both reminds the learner of the allowed answer set and prevents the trivial give-away of a long blank.

When one cause drives several values at once, group them under a single c-index so they reveal together: `Reticulocyte count: {{c1::↑::↑/↓}}` / `Bilirubin: {{c1::↑::↑/↓}}` / `Hgb: {{c1::↓::↑/↓}}`. A grouped panel turns one disease into a full lab-profile prediction in a single card. You can also mix directions within one stem (`{{c1::increased}} in starvation and {{c1::decreased}} in obesity`) to contrast two conditions.

This differs from a plain fill-in-the-blank cloze in that the blank is deliberately a direction word, and from a definition card in that nothing is being named  -  the learner is reasoning to a vector. Reach for it whenever the testable fact is "which way does X move," especially for hormone/lab panels, drug effects, and physiologic compensation.

**Canonical syntax:** `<cause/condition> ... <analyte>? {{c1::Increased::↑ / ↓ / Normal}}  (cloze the direction; legend hint; group multi-analyte panels under one c1)`

**When to use:** Use when the fact being tested is which way a value moves (up, down, or unchanged) in response to a cause  -  hormone and lab panels, drug effects, and physiologic compensation. Especially powerful for grouping several analytes that a single condition shifts together.

**Watch out for:** Don't cloze the analyte and leave the direction showing  -  that inverts what you want to test. Always add a ↑/↓/normal legend hint so a short blank doesn't telegraph the answer, and include "Unchanged/Normal" as a real option so the learner can't reflexively guess up or down.

**Best practices**

- Cloze the direction word (Increased/Decreased/Unchanged), keep the analyte visible in the stem.
- Add a symbol-legend hint like ::↑ / ↓ / Normal or ::Increased/Decreased to define the answer set.
- Include 'Unchanged' / 'No change' as a genuine option when it's a real possibility  -  don't make every card a coin-flip.
- Group multiple analytes shifted by one cause under a single c1 so the whole panel reveals together.
- Mix directions across two conditions in one stem (↑ in A, ↓ in B) to teach contrast.
- Use the arrow glyphs (↑/↓) for compact panels; spell out 'Increased/Decreased' when the prose reads better.
- Put the 'why' (mechanism, feedback loop) in the EXTRA field, not the cloze.

**Worked examples (70)**

#### 12.1  one-word 'Increased' reveal for a hormone effect · physiology

**Raw `Text` field:**

```
<div>What is the effect of <b>sleep</b> on <b>growth hormone secretion</b>?</div><br><div>{{c1::Increased}}</div>
```

**Reads as →**

What is the effect of sleep on growth hormone secretion?

【Increased】

**`Extra` field →**

Specifically, stage III and IV sleep

| Stimulatory Factors | Inhibitory Factors |
| --- | --- |
| ↓ Glucose | ↑ Glucose |
| ↓ FFA | ↑ FFA |
| Fasting | Obesity |
| Exercise | GH |
| Stress | Obesity |
| Sleep | Senescence |
| α-adrenergic agonists | Pregnancy |
| Sex hormones | Somatostatin |

> **Why it works:** Cleanest possible form: cause + analyte in the stem, direction is the whole answer.

```

Causes striae (stretch marks)

#### 12.4  arrow-glyph cause → {{c1::↑}} risk in an equation-style stem · physiology

**Raw `Text` field:**

```
↓ <b>Dietary calcium</b> = {{c1::↑}} risk of <u>calcium oxalate stones</u>
```

**Reads as →**

↓ Dietary calcium = 【↑】 risk of calcium oxalate stones

**`Extra` field →**

- Calcium binds with oxalate in the gut to form unabsorbable calcium oxalate

- Therefore, reduced dietary calcium leads to an increase in oxalate absorption in the gut, which is then excreted into the urine and binds urinary calcium to form calcium oxalate stones

- Excess calcium supplementation (i.e., not from food sources) is also associated with increased stone formation

> **Why it works:** Uses ↓ in the stem and clozes the bare ↑ glyph, the most compact direction form.

```

Increased cortisol levels lead to 【decreased】 immunologic function.

**`Extra` field →**

increased stress → increased cortisol → weakened immune system

> **Why it works:** Direction-in, direction-out: a visible ↑ cause with the clozed ↓ consequence.

#### 12.8  counterintuitive serum K+ with Increased/Decreased legend hint · physiology

**Raw `Text` field:**

```
What is the typical <b><u>serum</u> potassium</b> level in a newly diagnosed patient with <b>T1DM</b>?<br><br>{{c1::Increased::Increased or Decreased}}
```

**Reads as →**

What is the typical serum potassium level in a newly diagnosed patient with T1DM?

【Increased ⟨hint: Increased or Decreased⟩】

**`Extra` field →**

- NOTE: Despite elevated serum potassium, intracellular potassium stores are low, so total body potassium may be low

- When treated with insulin, K^(+) rapidly shifts from the extracellular space back into cells potentially resulting in a dangerously low serum K^(+) (hypokalemia)

- Insulin shifts K^(+) into the cells. Low or absent insulin in T1DM may lead to high serum (extracellular) K^(+) and low intracellular/total body K^(+). This may be further exacerbated by the K^(+)-H^(+) exchanger as it tries to compensate in an acidotic state (e.g., DKA)

> **Why it works:** Legend hint forces a real choice on a value most learners guess wrong.

- Although uncommon, the condition may require surgical intervention, affecting only 1% of the US dialysis population each year

#### 12.24  graph reasoning: Y-intercept ↑ means V_max {{c1::decreased}} · biochem/physics

**Raw `Text` field:**

```
<div>If the <b>Y-intercept</b> <u>increases</u> on a Lineweaver-Burk plot, the <b>V<sub>max</sub> </b>has {{c1::decreased}}</div>
```

**Reads as →**

If the Y-intercept increases on a Lineweaver-Burk plot, the V_(max) has 【decreased】

**`Extra` field →**

- The Y-intercept represents \(\frac{1}{V_{max}}\) (where V_(max) is the maximum reaction velocity)

- An increase in the Y-intercept means that V_(max) has decreased since V_(max) is inversely proportional to the Y-intercept

 [image: c5f7510919d6ed56a5e37d7e87d1ded9.webp]

> **Why it works:** Inverse-relationship direction inference from a Lineweaver-Burk plot.

#### 12.34  Hypoventilation = unchanged A-a gradient, ↔ cloze with ↑↓↔ hint · physiology

**Raw `Text` field:**

```
Hypoventilation = respiratory acidosis and {{c1::↔::↑↓↔}} A-a gradient
```

**Reads as →**

Hypoventilation = respiratory acidosis and 【↔ ⟨hint: ↑↓↔⟩】 A-a gradient

**`Extra` field →**

- A-a gradient < 15
- Hypoventilation = ↓ pH + ↑ P_(a)CO_(2) + ↓ P_(a)O_(2)

- The A-a gradient measures oxygen transfer from the lungs to the blood and can help determine the cause of low blood oxygen levels. To calculate it, the alveolar oxygen tension (PAO2) is first determined using a specific equation: PAO2 = (FiO2 x [Patm - PH20]) - (PaCO2/R)= (0.21 × [760-47]) - (59/0.8) = 76

- The A-a gradient is then calculated by A-a gradient = PAO2 - PaO2 = 76 - 62 = 14

- A normal A-a gradient is less than 15, and anything above 30 is considered elevated regardless of age

 [image: 58a47d34a9d3ee2f262d07a99dfabd81.webp]

> **Why it works:** Teaches the 'no change' (↔) option alongside up/down via a three-symbol legend.

How does oral estrogen change the required therapeutic dose of levothyroxine in patients with hypothyroidism?

- Therefore need to increase dose to saturate new TBG binding sites

# Part IV - The Extra Field (the teaching half)

_Everything below the answer line. The front TESTS one thing; the Extra TEACHES the context, mechanism, and memory hooks around it._


## 13. The Extra Field as the Teaching Half

An AnKing cloze note has two halves that do different jobs. The **front** (the text containing the `{{c1::...}}` deletions) is a *test*: it should isolate exactly one recallable fact and nothing more. The **Extra field** is the *teacher*: it carries the mechanism, the why, the caveats, the comparisons, and the exceptions that you should read on every review but never have to actively recall. Mastering this technique means deliberately deciding what goes on which side. If a clause explains *why* the answer is true, it almost always belongs in the Extra, not buried in the front.

The cloze syntax itself is ordinary  -  `{{c1::answer}}` for a plain deletion, `{{c1::answer::hint}}` when you want a disambiguating cue on the masked blank, e.g. `treated with a(n) {{c1::ACE inhibitor::drug}}`. What distinguishes this technique is not the syntax but the *division of labor*: the front stays lean (one fact, sometimes a tight question-and-answer like `What is the next step...? {{c1::Bronchoalveolar lavage}}`), while the Extra does the heavy explanatory lifting. A good Extra reads like a concise textbook margin note: it states the mechanism (`Recurrent/severe episodes → less epinephrine released → fewer symptoms`), gives the contrast card (`compare with true gynecomastia, in which the margin of glandular tissue is palpable`), or lists the rule the answer is one instance of (`Diamagnetic = NO unpaired electrons... Paramagnetic = have unpaired electrons...`).

This differs from sibling techniques in a precise way. It is NOT the *mnemonic-expansion* card (where the Extra merely spells out an acronym you clozed)  -  here the Extra teaches genuine understanding, not just a memory peg. It is NOT *multi-cloze enumeration* (where several `{{cN::}}` blanks carry the whole content)  -  here a single short blank is paired with rich prose. And it is the opposite of a *self-contained one-liner* with an empty Extra. Use this when the fact is testable in one breath but only makes sense against a paragraph of context.

**Canonical syntax:** Front: lean stem with one `{{c1::answer}}` (optionally `::hint`). Extra: prose that gives mechanism / why / contrast / caveats  -  read every review, never recalled.

**When to use:** Use when the testable fact is short and crisp but would be confusing or rote without surrounding mechanism, comparison, or exceptions. Push the 'why' and the 'compare-with' into the Extra so the front tests one thing cleanly.

**Watch out for:** Don't cram the explanation into the front (it becomes a paragraph with one blank, diluting the test). Don't leave the Extra empty when the fact has a non-obvious mechanism. And don't make the Extra so dependent on an image that it teaches nothing as text.

**Best practices**

- Keep the front to a single recallable fact; if you find yourself writing 'because...' on the front, move that clause to the Extra.
- Make the Extra teach the mechanism with an explicit causal chain (use arrows: cause → effect → effect) so the answer feels inevitable rather than memorized.
- Add a 'compare with' line in the Extra for the nearest look-alike entity, so review reinforces the discriminating feature.
- Put exceptions, caveats, and 'do NOT' warnings in the Extra (e.g., 'elevated creatinine is NOT a contraindication'), where they're seen but not tested.
- Let the Extra carry numbers, doses, second-/third-line options, and worked examples that would overload the front.
- Use a `::hint` on the front only to disambiguate the blank ('::drug', '::Hormone', 'fast or slow'); keep the real teaching in the Extra, not the hint.
- Ensure the Extra still reads as complete prose if every image were removed  -  the text should teach on its own.

**Worked examples (175)**

#### 13.1  One-word cloze; Extra gives the etymology peg + the mechanism of decreased uptake · endocrine/thyroid

**Raw `Text` field:**

```
<u>Painful / tender thyroid</u> with {{c1::<u>decreased</u>}} radioactive iodine uptake is seen in <b>subacute granulomatous thyroiditis</b> (de Quervain)
```

**Reads as →**

Painful / tender thyroid with 【decreased】 radioactive iodine uptake is seen in subacute granulomatous thyroiditis (de Quervain)

**`Extra` field →**

- De QuerVAIN = PAIN

- Decreased uptake due to damaged thyroid follicular cells and initial thyrotoxic stage with negative feedback

> **Why it works:** Minimal front (a single 'decreased') paired with an Extra that both anchors the name and explains the radioactive-iodine physiology - the cleanest illustration of test-one-thing / teach-the-rest.

#### 13.2  Short diagnostic cloze; Extra adds epidemiology and risk factors · geriatrics/social

**Raw `Text` field:**

```
Older patient with <u>unexplained</u> change in <b>health status</b>, <b>behavior</b>, and/or <b>financial status</b> is concerning for {{c1::elder abuse}}
```

**Reads as →**

Older patient with unexplained change in health status, behavior, and/or financial status is concerning for 【elder abuse】

**`Extra` field →**

- Most common in women

- ↑ Risk in patients with dementia or chronic mental illness

#### 13.3  Treatment cloze; Extra gives course, escalation, and a 'do not' warning · dermatology/peds

**Raw `Text` field:**

```
What is the <u>treatment</u> for <b>neonatal cephalic pustulosis</b>?<br><br>{{c1::Observation + gentle soap and water}}
```

**Reads as →**

What is the treatment for neonatal cephalic pustulosis?

【Observation + gentle soap and water】

**`Extra` field →**

- Usually resolves within weeks to months; topical ketoconazole (or corticosteroid) if severe

- Avoid topical emollients!

> **Why it works:** Shows the Extra carrying a clinical caveat ('Avoid topical emollients!') that you should see but never have to recall.

#### 13.4  One-word risk-factor cloze; Extra quantifies the risk and explains why · oncology/GI

**Raw `Text` field:**

```
History of <u>childhood abdominal tumor</u> treated with {{c1::radiation}} warrants <b>early colorectal cancer screening</b>
```

**Reads as →**

History of childhood abdominal tumor treated with 【radiation】 warrants early colorectal cancer screening

**`Extra` field →**

- Estimated risk > 4x higher than general population of developing colon adenocarcinoma in adulthood

- Increased mutations in colonic mucosa, chronic inflammatory changes, and underlying genetic susceptibility

---
#### 13.5  Binary cloze (worsens/improves) with hint; Extra is a tight causal chain · endocrine

**Raw `Text` field:**

```
<b>Hypoglycemia awareness</b> {{c1::worsens::improves/worsens}} in patients with diabetes who have <u>recurrent</u> or <u>severe</u> hypoglycemia
```

**Reads as →**

Hypoglycemia awareness 【worsens ⟨hint: improves/worsens⟩】 in patients with diabetes who have recurrent or severe hypoglycemia

**`Extra` field →**

Recurrent/severe episodes → less epinephrine released (weaker autonomic response) → fewer symptoms & less awareness of hypoglycemia → cycle repeats itself

> **Why it works:** The front tests a single direction; the Extra's arrow-chain mechanism makes that direction feel inevitable rather than arbitrary.

---
#### 13.6  Drug-class cloze with ::drug hint; Extra holds pathophysiology cascade + a counterintuitive caveat · rheumatology/renal

**Raw `Text` field:**

```
<b>Acute scleroderma renal crisis</b> leads to <u>malignant hypertension</u> and is treated with a(n) {{c1::ACE inhibitor::drug}}
```

**Reads as →**

Acute scleroderma renal crisis leads to malignant hypertension and is treated with a(n) 【ACE inhibitor ⟨hint: drug⟩】

**`Extra` field →**

- Systemic sclerosis → collagen deposition → renal ischemia → RAAS activation → HTN → further renal ischemia

- Untreated may lead to HF, MI, renal insufficiency, stroke

- ACE inhibitors (e.g., captopril) treat HTN

- In scleroderma renal crisis, elevated serum creatinine level is NOT a contraindication for ACE inhibitors!

> **Why it works:** Model case: front is one drug class, Extra delivers the RAAS cascade AND the high-yield exception that elevated creatinine is not a contraindication.

---
#### 13.7  Single-concept cloze; Extra lists route, outcomes, and the contraindication exception · critical care/nutrition

**Raw `Text` field:**

```
In <b>critically-ill patients</b>, {{c1::enteral feeding}} is the optimal form of <u>nutrition</u>
```

**Reads as →**

In critically-ill patients, 【enteral feeding】 is the optimal form of nutrition

**`Extra` field →**

- Feed by nasogastric, orogastric, or postpyloric tube (ideally within 48 hours)

- Lower rate of infection, lower mortality rate

- Only give TPN if there is contraindication to EN

 [image: e8aa706b8e113c484baa3ffe3aa91524.webp]

#### 13.8  Sequencing cloze (glucose before CT); Extra explains both why-first and the mimic · neurology

**Raw `Text` field:**

```
For patients with <b>suspected stroke</b>, {{c1::rapid blood glucose}} should <u>precede</u> CT scan
```

**Reads as →**

For patients with suspected stroke, 【rapid blood glucose】 should precede CT scan

**`Extra` field →**

- Delays in correcting hypoglycemia can lead to acute clinical deterioration and worsen neurologic outcomes

- Hypoglycemia can also mimic stroke, so it is important to rule out

 [image: 77bf1b1a46bb42eeaaa4a141f286c9ef.webp]

> **Why it works:** Tests one ordering fact while the Extra teaches the two distinct reasons (deterioration risk + stroke mimic) behind it.

#### 13.9  Next-step-in-diagnosis cloze; Extra encodes the clinical-suspicion rule and a definition · toxicology/neuro

**Raw `Text` field:**

```
What is the <i>next step</i> in diagnosis for a <i>young</i> patient with <b>hemorrhagic stroke</b> and no chronic risk factors? Physical exam shows <b>HTN</b>, <b>tachycardia</b>, <b>mydriasis</b>, and <b>hyperthermia</b><br><br>

{{c1::Urine toxicology screen}}
```

**Reads as →**

What is the next step in diagnosis for a young patient with hemorrhagic stroke and no chronic risk factors? Physical exam shows HTN, tachycardia, mydriasis, and hyperthermia

【Urine toxicology screen】

**`Extra` field →**

- Suspect cocaine as the cause of intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) when stroke occurs in subcortical location and/or in young patients with associated sympathetic activation or absence of typical risk factors

- "Stroke in young patient" is generally defined as age < 45 years

**Raw `Text` field:**

Diagnosis of {{c2::<b>Waldenstr</b><b>ö</b><b>m macroglobulinemia</b>}} is <u>confirmed</u> via bone marrow biopsy showing {{c1::<b>&gt; 10% clonal <u>B cells</u></b>}}

Whereas multiple myeloma is confirmed by bone marrow biopsy showing > 10% clonal plasma cells

 [image: c4bd89a1bb070322892e5675afd462b3.webp]

#### 13.11  Diagnosis cloze; Extra gives the diagnostic-therapeutic trick plus a distinguishing feature · neurology/pharm

**Raw `Text` field:**

```
What is the most likely <u>diagnosis</u> in a patient with history of an <b>intermittent</b>, <b>high-frequency tremor</b> that worsens with stress who now has <b>more persistent/severe</b> presentation since starting an <u>SSRI</u>?<br><br>{{c1::Enhanced physiologic tremor}}
```

**Reads as →**

What is the most likely diagnosis in a patient with history of an intermittent, high-frequency tremor that worsens with stress who now has more persistent/severe presentation since starting an SSRI?

【Enhanced physiologic tremor】

**`Extra` field →**

- Dose reduction or stoppage of the offending medication can be both diagnostic and therapeutic

- Does not decrease with distraction (compare with functional tremor which does)

- Enhanced physiologic tremor may arise due to medications, physiologic conditions (stress, anxiety), or medical conditions (hypoglycemia, substance withdrawal, thyrotoxicosis, liver disease)

 [image: 4e1b36630388d58308c83408afe65984.webp]

#### 13.12  Long-vignette diagnosis cloze; Extra defines the entity against its true look-alike · endocrine/surgery

**Raw `Text` field:**

```
What is the most likely diagnosis in an <u>obese male</u> with <b>diffuse enlargement</b> of the breasts <b>without pain, nodules, or skin dimpling</b>? Patient denies nipple discharge, headaches, or erectile dysfunction<br><br>{{c1::Pseudogynecomastia / lipomastia}}
```

**Reads as →**

What is the most likely diagnosis in an obese male with diffuse enlargement of the breasts without pain, nodules, or skin dimpling? Patient denies nipple discharge, headaches, or erectile dysfunction

【Pseudogynecomastia / lipomastia】

**`Extra` field →**

- Excessive deposition of fat in the breast, commonly extending into the axilla and skin folds without a distinct margin; compare with true gynecomastia, in which the margin of glandular tissue is palpable and the breast may be tender

- Clinical diagnosis, no further workup required in the absence of hypogonadal or pituitary symptoms; next step is weight loss (liposuction or surgical reduction can be considered)

 [image: 5f9d1acd0ca192dbb15ef19ed3f3599c.svg]
 [image: fb98424e15371c58617ac07722eb6809.svg]

Last updated: April 20, 2024

> **Why it works:** Front is a one-shot diagnosis; Extra explicitly contrasts pseudogynecomastia with true gynecomastia, the highest-yield teaching move.

#### 13.13  Diagnosis cloze; Extra covers mechanism, presentation, and confirmatory test · hematology/transfusion

**Raw `Text` field:**

```
What is the most likely <u>diagnosis</u> in a patient who presents <i>days to weeks</i> <u>post-transfusion</u> with <b>worsening Hb</b> after initial improvement and laboratory evidence of <b>hemolysis</b>?<br><br>{{c1::Delayed hemolytic transfusion reaction (DHTR)}}
```

**Reads as →**

What is the most likely diagnosis in a patient who presents days to weeks post-transfusion with worsening Hb after initial improvement and laboratory evidence of hemolysis?

【Delayed hemolytic transfusion reaction (DHTR)】

**`Extra` field →**

- Antibody response to minor RBC antigens → increased risk in patients requiring frequent transfusion (sickle cell disease, thalassemia) due to alloimmunization from frequent transfusions

- Presents as fatigue, dyspnea, jaundice, and low-grade fever with increased indirect bilirubin, LDH, and reticulocyte count

- Diagnosis requires a new positive Coombs test

 [image: c44aa200e0ab215b6c9da718be6df2d3.webp]

---
#### 13.14  Counterintuitive next-step cloze ('no management'); Extra justifies the non-action with three reasons · OB/GYN

**Raw `Text` field:**

```
What is the <i>next step</i> in management of <u>asymptomatic</u> <b>bacterial vaginosis</b> detected by cytology?<br><br>{{c1::No additional management}}
```

**Reads as →**

What is the next step in management of asymptomatic bacterial vaginosis detected by cytology?

【No additional management】

**`Extra` field →**

- Pap test cytology has low sensitivity and low specificity for identifying BV! High false positive rate!

Do not treat asymptomatic BV anyways because:
- It may resolve spontaneously
- Treatment can lead to symptomatic vaginal candidiasis

**`Extra` field →**

Each mass is multiplied by the isotope's natural abundance

Carbon 13 (C13) → 1% abundance = 0.01;

```

He atom is 【diamagnetic ⟨hint: diamagnetic or paramagnetic⟩】.

**`Extra` field →**

- Diamagnetic materials = NO unpaired electrons and weakly repelled by a magnetic field (e.g., He, Be, Zn)
- Paramagnetic materials =  have unpaired electrons and weakly attracted by a magnetic field, cannot retain magnetism when field removed (e.g., Al)
- Ferromagnetic materials = have unpaired electrons and strongly attracted by a magnetic field, can retain magnetism when field removed (e.g., Fe, Ni, Co)

**Reads as →**

The most serious side effect of metformin is 【lactic acidosis】

**`Extra` field →**

- When you inhibit hepatic gluconeogenesis, you inhibit lactate's ability to enter hepatic gluconeogenesis - therefore lactate builds up in serum

- This can be fatal and is more likely to occur in hypoxic tissues (these tissues will have switched over to anaerobic glycolysis and therefore are more susceptible)

> **Why it works:** Rich Extra walks the full causal chain from gluconeogenesis inhibition to fatal lactate accumulation.

#### 13.55  Mg hydroxide antacid toxicity; Extra details VDCC/CaSR mechanisms behind hypotension · pharmacology

**Raw `Text` field:**

```
<div><i><div></div></i></div>Which <u>antacid</u> is associated with <b>hyporeflexia</b>,<b> hypotension</b>, and <b>cardiac arrest</b> if overused?<br><br><div>{{c1::Magnesium hydroxide}}</div>
```

**Reads as →**

Which antacid is associated with hyporeflexia, hypotension, and cardiac arrest if overused?

【Magnesium hydroxide】

**`Extra` field →**

- Magnesium stabilizes VDCCs on neuromuscular junctions → neuromuscular toxicity

- Magnesium activates CaSR (calcium-sensing receptor), resulting in decreased PTH → decreased Ca^(2+) (Ca^(2+) is needed for vasoconstriction) → hypotension

- Hyperkalemia (high extracellular K^(+)) results in depolarization without the ability to repolarize; v-gated Na^(+) can't be reset, resulting in inhibition of Na^(+) channels and the inability to generate a new contraction (which leads to cardiac arrest)

> **Why it works:** Front is a single drug name; Extra unpacks several distinct mechanisms for the toxicity triad.

#### 13.94  metformin activates AMPK, Extra explains why no hypoglycemia · biochem/pharm

**Raw `Text` field:**

```
<div>One mechanism by which <b>metformin</b> decreases gluconeogenesis is via {{c2::<u>activation</u>}} of the enzyme {{c1::<b><i>AMP-activated protein kinase</i></b> (AMPK)}}<br></div>
```

**Reads as →**

One mechanism by which metformin decreases gluconeogenesis is via 【c2: activation】 of the enzyme 【c1: AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK)】

**`Extra` field →**

- AMPK is an enzyme which protects cells from a lack of ATP (energy deficiency) by increasing cellular uptake of glucose and fatty acid oxidation.
- Therefore, it does not provoke hypoglycemia because it increases insulin sensitivity not release (release is still regulated by endogenous regulation)

- Metformin also decreases gluconeogenesis via inhibition of the mitochondrial enzyme glycerol-3-phosphate dehydrogenase (mGPD)

#### 13.116  PPV increases intrathoracic pressure, decreases RV preload, Extra explains sudden cardiac death · physio

**Raw `Text` field:**

```

```

**Reads as →**

Positive pressure mechanical ventilation causes an acute 【c1: increase ⟨hint: increase/decrease⟩】 in intrathoracic pressure, which 【c1: decreases ⟨hint: increases/decreases⟩】 RV preload by compressing the IVC

**`Extra` field →**

- Loss of RV preload can lead to sudden cardiac death
- In the setting of decreased CVP (e.g., hypovolemic shock) → acute loss of RV preload can result in sudden cardiac death

- Decreased RV preload & increased intrathoracic pressure (RV afterload) → decreased LV preload
- Decreased MAP (baroreceptor effect) & decreased LV transmural pressure → decreased LV afterload

#### 13.169  ITP second-line IVIG/anti-Rho(D); Extra explains splenic macrophage decoy mechanism · pathology

**Raw `Text` field:**

```
What is the next step in treating a patient with <b><u>immune</u> thrombocytopenia</b> (ITP) and a <b>platelet count &lt; 30,000/µL</b> who <u>does not</u> respond to <u>corticosteroids</u>?<br><br>{{c1::IVIG}} or {{c1::anti-Rho(D) immunoglobulin if Rh+}}
```

**Reads as →**

What is the next step in treating a patient with immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) and a platelet count < 30,000/µL who does not respond to corticosteroids?

【c1: IVIG】 or 【c1: anti-Rho(D) immunoglobulin if Rh+】

**`Extra` field →**

- First-line is corticosteroids

- If there is no response to, contraindication to, or intolerance of corticosteroids: treat with IVIG or anti-Rho(D) immunoglobulin

- Anti-Rho(D) is used to intentionally overwhelm the patient's splenic macrophages (which are too preoccupied with destroying anti-Rho(D)–tagged RBCs to destroy platelets). Used very sparingly because it can cause life-threatening anemia

 [image: 753d443cb002375ee5a7936cf6530e6a.webp]

> **Why it works:** Extra gives a vivid mechanistic picture of why anti-Rho(D) spares platelets.

#### 13.171  Postpartum shock + purple vaginal mass = vaginal hematoma; Extra explains occult blood loss physiology · pathology

**Raw `Text` field:**

```
What is the most likely <i>diagnosis</i> in a postpartum patient who develops <b>shock</b> with <b>minimal bleeding</b>, a <b>palpable uterus</b>, and a <b>purple vaginal mass</b>?<br><br><div>{{c1::Vaginal hematoma}}<br></div>
```

**Reads as →**

What is the most likely diagnosis in a postpartum patient who develops shock with minimal bleeding, a palpable uterus, and a purple vaginal mass?

【Vaginal hematoma】

**`Extra` field →**

- Can cause life-threatening occult blood loss as the uterine artery enlarges in pregnancy and supplies the uterus with up to 30% of cardiac output

- Sometimes associated with a protruding vaginal mass

- Usually due to uncontrolled delivery or assisted vaginal delivery (forceps or vacuum)

- Treatment depends on its progression and may require embolization / surgery if it is expanding

## 14. Mnemonics & Memory Aids

Mnemonics & Memory Aids cards weld a memory hook to the fact so that recalling the card and recalling the device become one act. There are two dominant structures. In the FIRST, the mnemonic IS the answer: the stem describes a list or grouping and asks you to recall the acronym, so you cloze the acronym itself, e.g. `Clinical features of infective endocarditis may be remembered with the mnemonic {{c1::FROM JANE}}`. The full expansion of the letters lives in the Extra field. In the SECOND, the fact is the answer and the mnemonic is a cue that lives in the Extra field (or as a 'remember…/think of…' phrase), reinforcing recall without being tested, e.g. clozing `{{c1::parasympathetic nervous system}}` while the Extra says 'Remember P for Parasympathetic: Piña colada on the beach.'

The exact cloze syntax is the standard `{{c1::answer}}`, optionally with a hint: `{{c1::answer::hint}}`. A powerful variant pairs an acronym stem with an enumerated, first-letter-hinted list, all under one cloze group, so each blank shows its initial letter as the hint: `{{c1::Retinopathy of prematurity::R}}`. Here the first letters spell the mnemonic, and the hint both scaffolds recall AND teaches the device. Use `<div class="mnemonics">` to wrap such lists when imitating AnKing structure.

Reach for this technique whenever the underlying content is an arbitrary, order-or-membership list (hormones, enzymes, branches, steps, criteria) that has no internal logic to lean on. The mnemonic supplies the missing structure. It differs from a plain list-cloze (which just blanks the items) by attaching a retrieval handle; it differs from a hint-only card because the hint here is specifically a memory device (an initial letter spelling a word, or an evocative image) rather than a neutral disambiguator.

Decide deliberately where the device goes. Cloze the acronym when the test-worthy skill is 'recall the mnemonic, then unpack it.' Keep the device in Extra (or as 'think of…') when the test-worthy skill is the fact itself and the mnemonic is merely a crutch you want present but not quizzed.

**Canonical syntax:** `{{c1::ACRONYM}} with the expansion in Extra  -  or {{c1::fact}} with a 'remember…/think of…' device in Extra; for spelled-out lists use {{c1::Item::FirstLetter}} per line`

**When to use:** Use for arbitrary lists, groupings, criteria, or ordered steps that lack internal logic, where an acronym or vivid image is the realistic path to recall. Choose between clozing the acronym itself versus keeping the device in Extra based on whether the mnemonic or the fact is what you actually want tested.

**Watch out for:** Don't cloze both the acronym AND every expanded item on the same card unless you intend a multi-step drill  -  pick the level you want tested. Avoid burying a mnemonic in Extra when the card's whole point is recalling that mnemonic, and don't invent a device so strained it is harder to remember than the raw list.

**Best practices**

- When the acronym is the answer, cloze the acronym and put the full letter-by-letter expansion in Extra so the back teaches what each letter stands for.
- When the fact is the answer, keep the mnemonic in Extra or as a 'Remember…/Think of…' phrase so it reinforces without being tested.
- For spelled-out lists, give each item a first-letter hint (`{{c1::Fever::F}}`) so the hints themselves reconstruct the acronym.
- Group the expanded items under one cloze number (all c1) when they are an unordered set, so the whole list is revealed together.
- Make image/word-association devices concrete and sensory ('sticky sugars cause sticky shoulders', 'Pseudomonas air-uginosa')  -  vividness drives retention.
- State explicitly in the stem that a mnemonic exists ('may be remembered with the mnemonic …') so the learner knows a device is the expected retrieval path.
- Keep the expansion ordered to match the acronym's letters so the Extra reads as a clean key.

**Worked examples (82)**

#### 14.1  Word-play device in Extra, fact is clozed · microbiology

**Raw `Text` field:**

```
{{c1::<i>Pseudomonas aeruginosa</i>}} is a gram-negative nosocomial bacterial infection that has <b>respiratory therapy equipment</b> as a risk factor
```

**Reads as →**

【Pseudomonas aeruginosa】 is a gram-negative nosocomial bacterial infection that has respiratory therapy equipment as a risk factor

**`Extra` field →**

Think of Pseudomonas "air"-uginosa when air or burns are involved

> **Why it works:** Shows the simplest form: the answer is the organism and the Extra carries a pun ('air-uginosa') that hooks the risk factor without being tested.

#### 14.8  Per-item silly-phrase mnemonic in Extra · molecular biology

**Raw `Text` field:**

```
<div><u>Initiation (start) Codon</u>:&nbsp;{{c1::AUG}}<br></div><br><div><i>Termination (stop) Codons</i>:&nbsp;{{c1::UAA}},&nbsp;{{c1::UGA}},&nbsp;{{c1::UAG}}</div>
```

**Reads as →**

Initiation (start) Codon: 【c1: AUG】

Termination (stop) Codons: 【c1: UAA】, 【c1: UGA】, 【c1: UAG】

**`Extra` field →**

Mnemonic:

AUG - the start of school
UAA - u are annoying
UGA - u go away
UAG - u are gone

Depending on study resource, stop codons may be called "amber" codons. 
But other names also exist: amber (UAG), ochre (UAA), and opal (UGA). Important Note
An open reading frame begins with a start codon (AUG) and ends with a stop codon (UAA, UAG, or UGA). The start and stop codons must be in the same reading frame that is set by the Start codon. 

Khan Academy Link

> **Why it works:** Start/stop codons get an individual phrase each ('UAA - u are annoying'), showing mnemonics tailored item-by-item.

C - OCPD, Dependent, Avoidant

| Type of Disorder | Cluster A | Cluster B | Cluster C |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Personality Disorder Examples | Paranoid Personality DisorderSchizoid Personality DisorderSchizotypal Personality Disorder | Antisocial Personality DisorderBorderline Personality DisorderHistrionic Personality Disorder | Avoidant Personality DisorderDependent Personality DisorderObsessive-Compulsive Personality Disorder |
| Explanation | Cluster A personality disorders are characterized by eccentric and odd behaviors, including suspiciousness, detachment, and social isolation. | Cluster B personality disorders are marked by dramatic, emotional, and erratic behaviors, including impulsivity, instability, and attention-seeking. | Cluster C personality disorders involve anxious and fearful behaviors, including avoidance, dependency, and perfectionism. |
| Example | Someone with paranoid personality disorder may exhibit excessive distrust and suspicion of others. | Someone with antisocial personality disorder may display a lack of regard for the rights of others and engage in manipulative or deceitful behavior. | Someone with avoidant personality disorder may experience extreme anxiety and avoid social interactions due to fear of rejection or criticism. |

#### 14.34  Charge/binding reasoning aid in Extra · biochemistry

**Raw `Text` field:**

```
<b><i>2,3-BPG</i>&nbsp;</b>causes heme to&nbsp;{{c1::release}} O<sub style="">2</sub>.
```

**Reads as →**

**`Extra` field →**

Creates a right shift just like a low pH would

 [image: 1a6f16a5109071f73225497e04d9a34a.webp]

 
2,3 BPG is an isomer of an intermediate in glycolysis (1,3-BPG) with two phosphate groups (note it's negative and when we exercise, a lot will be produced). So it can only bind to a hemoglobin without any of the four oxygen, it connects to two positive groups (remember 2,3 BPG is negative) and causes a conformational change that, when bound, causes hemoglobin to have a much lower affinity for oxygen.

#### 14.35  Equation as memory-consolidation anchor · physics/chemistry

**Raw `Text` field:**

```
Give the equation for the <b>ideal gas law</b>:<br><br><div>{{c1::\(PV=nRT\)}}</div>
```

**Reads as →**

Give the equation for the ideal gas law:

【\(PV=nRT\)】

**`Extra` field →**

P = pressure
V = volume
n = number of moles
R = gas constant
T = temperature

The ideal gas law is a combination of Boyle's law, Charles's law, Avogadro's law, and Gay-Lussac's law. Thus, you only need to memorize this one equation to remember all gas law relationships.

Boyle's Law: \(P_{1}V_{1} = P_{2}V_{2}\)

Charles's Law: \(\frac{V_{1} }{T_{1} } = \frac{V_{2} }{T_{2} }\)

Avogadro's law: \(\frac{V_{1} }{n_{1} } = \frac{V_{2} }{n_{2} }\)

Gay-Lussac's Law: \(\frac{P_{1} }{T_{1} } = \frac{P_{2} }{T_{2} }\)
Khan Academy Link

> **Why it works:** The single clozed equation (PV=nRT) is framed as the one thing to memorize because it subsumes the other gas laws.

Pressure (P)

Density (p)

Volume (V)

For example, whether you climb 10 flights of stairs or take an elevator up 10 floors the final destination will result in you having the same change in potential energy. 

Depends only on the present state of a system and not how the state was reached, nor on the history of the system

#### 14.70  LOT acronym for benzodiazepines safe in liver disease · pharmacology

**Raw `Text` field:**

```
<div>The {{c1::<b>benzodiazepines</b>}} that are <u><b>safe to use</b></u> in patients with <u>liver disease</u> may be remembered with the mnemonic "<b>LOT</b>":<br></div><div><div class="mnemonics"><br><div>{{c1::<u>L</u>orazepam::<b>L</b>}}</div><div>{{c1::<u>O</u>xazepam::<b>O</b>}}</div><div>{{c1::<u>T</u>emazepam::<b>T</b>}} </div></div></div>
```

**Reads as →**

The 【c1: benzodiazepines】 that are safe to use in patients with liver disease may be remembered with the mnemonic "LOT":

【c1: Lorazepam ⟨hint: L⟩】
【c1: Oxazepam ⟨hint: O⟩】
【c1: Temazepam ⟨hint: T⟩】

**`Extra` field →**

- Benzodiazepines are metabolized in the liver and then excreted in the urine

- Most benzodiazepines are metabolized via CYP-mediated hepatic oxidative reduction (phase I) followed by glucuronide conjugation (phase II)

- However, certain benzodiazepines (lorazepam, oxazepam, temazepam) undergo only glucuronide conjugation, which tends to be relatively preserved in the elderly and those with liver disease

# Part V - Card Archetypes: Question Patterns

_Recurring shapes that map a kind of knowledge (a definition, a contrast, an association, a pathway, an exception) onto the cloze mechanics from Part I._


## 15. Definition Cards

A definition card pairs a TERM with its DEFINING PROPERTY and clozes exactly one of the two, so the visible half cues recall of the hidden half. There are two directions, and a well-built card chooses deliberately. **Cloze the definition** (term shown) when you want "given the name, state what it is"  -  e.g. `{{c1::Ionization energy}} is the amount of energy required to {{c1::remove an electron}}` written as `Ionization energy is the amount of energy required to {{c1::remove an electron}}`. **Cloze the term** (definition shown) when you want "given the description, name it"  -  e.g. `{{c1::Koilocytes}} are a cytologic feature of HPV-infected cells with a 'raisin-like' nucleus`.

The single highest-leverage move in this technique is the **two-way definition**: put the term in `{{c1::...}}` and the defining clause in `{{c2::...}}`, producing one note that tests both directions as separate cards. The canonical shape is `{{c1::TERM}} is {{c2::DEFINING PROPERTY}}`  -  e.g. `{{c1::Electron affinity}} is {{c2::the amount of energy released when an electron is added to the atom}}`. Card 1 hides the term (recognition → name) and Card 2 hides the definition (name → meaning). This is the bread-and-butter pattern for vocabulary-style facts and is why so many of the strongest examples carry distinct=2.

Hints earn their keep here: append `::hint` to disambiguate (`{{c1::Rutherford Model::... Model}}` tells the learner a model name is wanted; `{{c1::diamagnetic::diamagnetic or paramagnetic}}` collapses a binary into a clean recall). Note types that read as complete sentences ("A/an {{c1::covalent}} bond is the {{c2::sharing}} of electrons between two atoms") beat bare "Term = ___" because the surrounding clause supplies the discriminating context.

This differs from neighboring techniques: it is NOT the question-and-answer/clinical-vignette pattern ("What is the likely diagnosis in a patient with...? {{c1::answer}}"), which tests application rather than the meaning of a word; and it is NOT enumeration/list cloze, which hides several coordinate members of one set. Definition cards always hinge on the term↔meaning relationship.

**Canonical syntax:** `{{c1::TERM}} is {{c2::DEFINING PROPERTY}}   -  cloze the term, the definition, or both (distinct c1/c2) to test either or both directions; add ::hint to disambiguate.`

**When to use:** Use for any term/definition or named-concept fact where the goal is to bind a label to its meaning. Reach for the two-way (c1 term / c2 definition) form whenever both directions are worth knowing; cloze a single side when only one direction is useful.

**Watch out for:** Don't cloze both the term AND its definition inside the SAME cloze number, or the card shows nothing but blanks and is unanswerable; use c1 vs c2 for the two halves. Avoid clozing a word so generic the surrounding sentence still gives it away, and add a ::hint when the blank could be filled by several plausible answers.

**Best practices**

- Write the full sentence first ("X is Y"), then decide which half to hide; the un-clozed half must be a sufficient cue on its own.
- For two-way recall put the term in {{c1::}} and the defining clause in {{c2::}} so one note yields both a name->meaning and a meaning->name card.
- Keep the definition clause tight and discriminating: hide the words that actually distinguish this term from its neighbors, not filler.
- Add ::hint to constrain open-ended blanks  -  a category cue (::Hormone, ::... Model) or an explicit binary (::reversible or irreversible).
- Prefer complete-sentence phrasing over bare 'Term = ___'; the carrier sentence supplies context and reads naturally on the answer side.
- When clozing the term, make the definition specific enough that exactly one term fits; vague descriptions produce ambiguous, ungradeable cards.
- Choose direction by utility: cloze the definition when learners know the word and need its meaning; cloze the term when they must produce the name from a description.

**Worked examples (158)**

```

**Reads as →**

【c1: Ionization energy】 is the amount of energy required to 【c2: remove an electron】.

**`Extra` field →**

#### 15.4  Definition with answer split: term in c1, multi-part defining clause in c2 · chemistry

**Raw `Text` field:**

```

```

**Reads as →**

【c1: Z_(eff)】 is the 【c2: attractive positive】 charge of 【c2: nuclear protons】 acting on 【c2: valence electrons】.

**`Extra` field →**

Z_(eff) (effective nuclear charge) is always less than the total number of protons present in a nucleus due to the shielding effect from other core electrons in the atom

Z_(eff) = Z - S
Z = nuclear charge (# of protons)
S = shielding constant (# of electrons between electrons of interest and nucleus)

| ms | electron spin | +1/2 and -1/2 |

#### 15.24  Single-cloze definition: subchorionic hemorrhage defined by location · OB/path

What is the greatest risk factor for primary nocturnal enuresis?

【Family history】

**`Extra` field →**

- Defined as nighttime urinary incontinence in a child ≥ 5 years old who has never achieved prolonged period (≥ 6 months) of dryness overnight

- Most patients have at least one parent who experienced enuresis as a child, and children with two parents who were affected are highly likely to develop the condition

- History and severity of enuresis also often follow the course experienced by the affected family member, with resolution expected around a similar age

#### 15.50  two-cloze definition of a virulence factor and its organism (Protein A) · micro

<b>{{c2::Protein A}}</b> is a <u>virulence factor</u> of<i> </i>{{c1::<i>Staphylococcus aureus</i>}}
```

【c2: Protein A】 is a virulence factor of 【c1: Staphylococcus aureus】

#### 15.51  two-cloze: drug name + its receptor mechanism (loperamide, mu-opioid) · pharm

**Raw `Text` field:**

```
<div>{{c1::<b>Loperamide</b>}} is a(n) {{c2::<b>μ-opioid</b>}} <b>agonist</b> that <b>does not</b> <b>cross</b> the BBB; therefore, there is no analgesia and low potential for addiction<br></div>
```

**Reads as →**

【c1: Loperamide】 is a(n) 【c2: μ-opioid】 agonist that does not cross the BBB; therefore, there is no analgesia and low potential for addiction

**`Extra` field →**

- At high doses, loperamide may cross the BBB & produce symptoms of opioid intoxication!

- Diphenoxylate is another μ-opioid agonist that crosses the BBB (& combined with atropine to prevent drug abuse)

#### 15.52  two-cloze: drug name + what it prevents (misoprostol / NSAID ulcers) · pharm

**Raw `Text` field:**

```
<div><b>{{c1::Misoprostol}}</b> is a PGE<sub>1</sub> analog that may be used to prevent <b>NSAID-induced {{c2::peptic ulcers}}</b><br></div>
```

**Reads as →**

【c1: Misoprostol】 is a PGE_(1) analog that may be used to prevent NSAID-induced 【c2: peptic ulcers】

**`Extra` field →**

NSAIDs block production of PGE_(1) at the stomach mucosa, which utilizes PGE_(1) to help vasodilate vessels that supply it (thus bringing more nutrients to help repair/grow)

---
#### 15.53  grouped cloze defining tertiary adrenal insufficiency's cause · pharm

**Raw `Text` field:**

```
<div>{{c2::<b>Tertiary</b>}}<b> adrenal insufficiency</b> is seen in patients with <u>chronic exogenous</u> {{c1::<b>glucocorticoid</b>}}<b> </b>use, precipitated by {{c1::<u>abrupt</u><b> withdrawal</b>}}</div>
```

**Reads as →**

【c2: Tertiary】 adrenal insufficiency is seen in patients with chronic exogenous 【c1: glucocorticoid】 use, precipitated by 【c1: abrupt withdrawal】

**`Extra` field →**

- Chronic exogenous steroids leads to a chronic suppression of ACTH release, leading to adrenal atrophy over time; thus discontinuing steroids abruptly leads to hypoadrenalism → tertiary from treatment
- Therefore chronic adrenal insufficiency patients who go for surgery are given a single dose of high dose steroids (stress dose steroids) to prevent insufficiency; also the basis for weaning patients off of steroids (slow discontinuation)

- Aldosterone synthesis is unaffected

 [image: b9b7c9d3c4ecf17bd5a813c1b55aa090.webp]

#### 15.55  cloze the named enzyme given mechanism context (AMPK / metformin) · pharm

**Raw `Text` field:**

```
<div>One mechanism by which <b>metformin</b> decreases gluconeogenesis is via {{c2::<u>activation</u>}} of the enzyme {{c1::<b><i>AMP-activated protein kinase</i></b> (AMPK)}}<br></div>
```

**Reads as →**

One mechanism by which metformin decreases gluconeogenesis is via 【c2: activation】 of the enzyme 【c1: AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK)】

**`Extra` field →**

- AMPK is an enzyme which protects cells from a lack of ATP (energy deficiency) by increasing cellular uptake of glucose and fatty acid oxidation.
- Therefore, it does not provoke hypoglycemia because it increases insulin sensitivity not release (release is still regulated by endogenous regulation)

- Metformin also decreases gluconeogenesis via inhibition of the mitochondrial enzyme glycerol-3-phosphate dehydrogenase (mGPD)

#### 15.121  Cloze the class given members (canagliflozin/dapagliflozin/empagliflozin = SGLT-2 inhibitors) · pharmacology

Canagliflozin, dapagliflozin, and empagliflozin are all examples of 【SGLT-2】 inhibitors

**`Extra` field →**

Weight loss, reduced risk of CAD / mortality related to heart failure

Steps that make SGLT-2 inhibitors renal protective:

- In diabetes, increased glucose filtration increases SGLT-2 transporters
- Increases in sodium concurrent reabsorption which leads to less sodium delivery to the macula densa
- This leads to increased renin release and hyperfiltration
- SGLT-2 inhibitors reduce this hyperfiltration by having more sodium reach the macula densa

```

**Reads as →**

What is the effect of hyperthyroidism on systemic vascular resistance?

【Decreased】

**`Extra` field →**

- Hyperthyroidism causes a T_(3) mediated peripheral vasodilation, but blood pressure (primarily systolic) rises due to positive inotropic and chronotropic effects

- In contrast, hypothyroidism causes hypertension due to an increase in systemic vascular resistance

## 16. Comparison Cards (X vs Y)

A comparison card sets two related entities (X and Y) side by side on a shared axis and clozes ONLY the distinguishing attribute, so the card forces you to recall the difference rather than the shared concept. The card body names both entities and states the axis explicitly; the answer is the value that separates them. Use parallel sentence structure so the contrast is obvious: "Compared to <X>, <Y> has {{c1::<distinguishing value>::hint}}" or "<X> does A whereas <Y> does B."

The core syntax is ordinary single-cloze: `Compared to hemoglobin, myoglobin has a much {{c1::higher::higher or lower}} affinity for oxygen`. The hint is invaluable here  -  a binary or small-set hint like `::higher or lower`, `::more/less`, `::↑↓`, or `::like or unlike` turns the card into a true discrimination task (the reader must commit to a direction, not just produce a plausible word). For two-sided definitions you can put one cloze on each side of the contrast: `{{c2::Cohesion}} refers to clinging of {{c1::like::like or unlike}} molecules ... {{c2::Adhesion}} refers to clinging of {{c1::unlike::like or unlike}} molecules`, reusing the same cloze number so the like/unlike pair is tested together.

This differs from a plain single-fact cloze (which has no second entity to contrast against) and from a list/enumeration card (which collects parallel members without pitting them against each other). The signature of a comparison card is the explicit comparator word  -  compared to, versus, whereas, rather than, as opposed to, unlike, greater/less than  -  paired with a cloze on the attribute that does the distinguishing.

**Canonical syntax:** `Compared to <X>, <Y> {{c1::<distinguishing attribute>::direction-hint}}  -  name both entities, state the axis, cloze only the difference.`

**When to use:** Use when two concepts are easily confused and the exam-relevant point is which one is higher/lower/earlier/present, not the shared definition. Ideal for paired pathologies, isomeric products, attachment styles, valve events, and any "X vs Y" the reader must keep straight in opposite directions.

**Watch out for:** Don't cloze the shared attribute or the entity name when the difference is the point  -  that tests recognition of the topic, not the contrast. Avoid leaving out the comparator (without "compared to Y" the card collapses into a plain fact), and always supply a small-set hint for directional answers so guessing is constrained.

**Best practices**

- Name BOTH entities and the shared axis in the stem; cloze only the value that differs.
- Add a constrained hint for directional answers: ::higher or lower, ::more/less, ::↑↓, ::earlier/later.
- Use strictly parallel phrasing for the two sides so the contrast reads cleanly.
- For symmetric pairs, make a card from each direction (X vs Y and Y vs X) so both are practiced.
- Reuse one cloze number across both halves of a two-sided definition to test the pair as a unit.
- Keep the comparator word explicit (compared to / whereas / unlike / rather than / greater than).
- Put the shared concept and any numbers/mnemonics in EXTRA rather than burying them in the cloze.

**Worked examples (78)**

#### 16.1  Single distinguishing attribute via 'Unlike' · neurophysiology

**Raw `Text` field:**

```
<u>Unlike</u> <i>proprioception</i>, <b>kinaesthesia </b>is {{c1::conscious}}.
```

**Reads as →**

Unlike proprioception, kinaesthesia is 【conscious】.

**`Extra` field →**

"If I move like this I will hit the baseball"

> **Why it works:** Cleanest minimal pattern: 'Unlike X, Y is {{c1::conscious}}' clozes exactly the one attribute that separates kinaesthesia from proprioception.

Compared to <u>tunneled central venous catheter</u>, <b>PICC lines</b> have {{c1::more::more/less}} {{c2::thrombotic}} events
```

Compared to tunneled central venous catheter, PICC lines have 【c1: more ⟨hint: more/less⟩】 【c2: thrombotic】 events

**`Extra` field →**

- Hickman catheter is a type of tunneled central venous catheter

- DVT usually seen within 1-2 weeks of PICC placement; presents as swelling ± pain and erythema

#### 16.35  Multi-line mitosis vs meiosis comparison grid · cell biology

**Raw `Text` field:**

```
Differences in <b>mitosis</b> vs <b>meiosis</b><br><br>- <b>Meiosis</b> results in {{c1::4::#}} daughter cells, while <b>mitosis</b> results in {{c1::2::#}} daughter cells<br>- <b>Meiosis</b> results in {{c1::haploid::haploid/diploid}} cells, while <b>mitosis</b> results in {{c1::diploid::haploid/diploid}} cells<br>- <b>Meiosis</b> occurs to form {{c1::gametes}}, while <b>mitosis</b> is for {{c1::growth/repair}}<br>- <b>Meiosis</b> results in cells that are {{c1::different::identical/different}} from parent cell, while <b>mitosis</b> results in cells that are {{c1::identical::identical/different}} to parent cell
```

**Reads as →**

Differences in mitosis vs meiosis

- Meiosis results in 【c1: 4 ⟨hint: #⟩】 daughter cells, while mitosis results in 【c1: 2 ⟨hint: #⟩】 daughter cells
- Meiosis results in 【c1: haploid ⟨hint: haploid/diploid⟩】 cells, while mitosis results in 【c1: diploid ⟨hint: haploid/diploid⟩】 cells
- Meiosis occurs to form 【c1: gametes】, while mitosis is for 【c1: growth/repair】
- Meiosis results in cells that are 【c1: different ⟨hint: identical/different⟩】 from parent cell, while mitosis results in cells that are 【c1: identical ⟨hint: identical/different⟩】 to parent cell

**`Extra` field →**

Meiosis occurs in gonadal cells to produce haploid sperm and egg cells that each contain 23 chromosomes and combine to form a diploid zygote. 

Oogenesis in females begins in the female embryo. Oocytes are frozen in metaphase II until fertilization.

Spermatogenesis in males does not begin until puberty.

**`One by one` field →** Y

#### 16.45  Fetal hemoglobin higher O2 affinity than adult · physiology

**Raw `Text` field:**

```
<b style="">Fetal hemoglobin</b> has a {{c1::higher::higher or lower}} affinity for oxygen compared to <i>adult hemoglobin.</i>
```

**Reads as →**

Fetal hemoglobin has a 【higher ⟨hint: higher or lower⟩】 affinity for oxygen compared to adult hemoglobin.

**`Extra` field →**

The result is fetal hemoglobin carries more O_(2) than adult hemoglobin
 [image: 2d15120b3aed9f833db17ee535b4380e.jpg]
Photo credit: Leticia, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

 [image: a19f1a0e21c8bad183a61c8496ae2f90.jpg]
Photo credit: Diberri (talk) (Uploads), CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

At all partial pressures, foetal haemoglobin has a greater affinity for oxygen. This makes sure that oxygen travels from the mother's blood via the placenta to the foetus.
Due to the high metabolic rate associated with foetal growth rates, the PO in foetal tissues is quite low.
Despite having a stronger affinity for oxygen in such a low partial pressure environment of the fetal tissue foetal haemoglobin readily unloads oxygen.
 At birth, adult-type haemoglobin replaces the foetal haemoglobin.

> **Why it works:** Cloze the affinity direction with a higher/lower cue; the compared pair frames the answer.

## 17. Buzzword & Classic-Association Cards

Buzzword and classic-association cards encode the single most testable link in medicine: a hallmark finding, pathognomonic clue, or "classically associated with" pairing maps to one diagnosis, drug, organism, or mechanism. The job of the card is to preserve the distinctive cue verbatim and cloze the thing it points to, so the learner trains the exact retrieval the exam tests: see the buzzword, name the answer.

The canonical pattern keeps the trigger fully exposed and clozes the linked term: `What herpesvirus is associated with {{c1::owl's eye inclusions}}?` is backwards; instead expose the buzzword and hide the association, e.g. `Which herpesvirus is associated with owl's eye inclusions? {{c1::CMV (HHV-5)}}` or, in prose form, `"Leonine facies" are characteristic of {{c1::lepromatous leprosy::which infection}}`. Use a hint when the answer space is large or ambiguous, with the `::` syntax: `{{c1::secretory::osmotic/secretory}} diarrhea`. The literal skeleton is `{{c1::answer::hint}}` where everything outside the braces stays as the recall cue.

Reach for this technique whenever a fact has a famous, unmistakable signature, a pathognomonic image-in-words (rust-colored sputum, beefy-red tongue, cigar-shaped yeast), a named eponym (Mackler triad, rule of 10s), or a textbook "X is associated with Y" sentence. Often the most efficient card clozes the diagnosis and leaves the finding visible, but you can also cloze the finding when the stem names the disease (`Graves disease is associated with {{c1::exophthalmos}}`) - choose whichever direction the buzzword actually cues on the exam.

This differs from a plain definition or mechanism card: you are not testing understanding of why, you are drilling the reflex association itself. It differs from a list/enumeration card because there is normally one tight answer, not an exhaustive set. Keep the buzzword intact, never cloze it away, or the card loses the very cue that makes the association learnable.

**Canonical syntax:** Keep the distinctive finding/buzzword exposed as the cue; cloze the linked diagnosis/drug/organism: `<buzzword> is associated with {{c1::answer::hint}}`

**When to use:** Use when a hallmark finding, pathognomonic clue, eponym, or "classically associated with" sentence maps to a single high-yield answer. Ideal for image-in-words descriptors and named triads.

**Watch out for:** Never cloze the buzzword itself - it must stay visible as the retrieval cue. Avoid clozing both the trigger and the answer in one blank so the card becomes guessable or directionless, and add a hint when the answer is one of several look-alikes.

**Best practices**

- Keep the distinctive finding (the buzzword) fully exposed; hide only the term it points to.
- Decide the direction: cloze the diagnosis when the finding is the cue, or the finding when the disease is named.
- Quote vivid image-in-words descriptors exactly ("rust-colored sputum", "owl's eye") - the wording is the cue.
- Add a `::hint` when the answer is one of a known set of confusables (osmotic/secretory, which fungus, severity).
- Use a single c1 for a tight one-fact link; split into c1/c2 only when two distinct associated facts are worth separate recall.
- Put the supporting mechanism or contrast in the EXTRA field, not in the stem, to keep the cue clean.
- Prefer the most specific buzzword available so the association is unambiguous rather than generic.

**Worked examples (88)**

#### 17.8  Graves -> exophthalmos / retro-orbital fibroblasts · physiology

**Reads as →**

Graves disease is associated with 【c1: exophthalmos】, which occurs due to activation of retro-orbital 【c2: fibroblasts】

**`Extra` field →**

- Activated T cells release cytokines (TNF-α, IFN-γ) which activate fibroblasts (along with TRAb to a lesser degree), causing increased secretions of glycosaminoglycans

- GAG deposition leads to osmotic muscle swelling, muscle inflammation, and increased adipocyte count → eyes being pushed out, dysfunction of extraocular muscles causes restricted extraocular movements and diplopia

- Visible appearance causes appearance of a "stare"

## 18. Mechanisms & Causal Chains

This technique clozes the LINK in a cause-and-effect relationship: the agent that acts, the direction of the effect (up vs. down, activates vs. inhibits, enhances vs. impairs), or the next node in a pathway. The card states a mechanism as a sentence (A leads to B; X activates Y; chronic alcohol downregulates Z) and hides exactly one load-bearing piece of that mechanism so the learner must recall the causal step rather than a free-floating fact. A literal minimal example: `Chronic alcohol use downregulates {{c1::GABA}} receptors and upregulates {{c1::NMDA glutamate}} receptors`  -  both ends of the contrast share the same `c1` so the card tests the paired mechanism as one idea.

The direction of effect is itself a frequent answer. When the trap is up/down or activate/inhibit, cloze the direction word and add a disambiguating cue: `is {{c3::activated::activated or inhibited}} by {{c1::ADP}} and {{c3::inhibited::activated or inhibited}} by {{c1::ATP}}`. The `::activated or inhibited` hint stops the answer from being given away by sentence grammar and forces a genuine binary recall. Use a cue like `::enhance/impair` or `::increase or decrease` whenever the blank would otherwise be guessable.

For a multi-step chain or an ordered pathway, give every step its own cloze. Use one shared group (all `c1`) when the steps are a single memorized set revealed together (e.g. an anatomical pathway `Ovary → Fallopian tube → Uterus → ...`, all `c1`), and use separate sequential groups (`c1`, `c2`, `c3`) when you want each link interrogated in isolation while the rest of the chain stays visible as scaffolding (e.g. `GnRH → anterior pituitary → FSH/LH`). Branching causes ("if mild → observe; if severe → antivenom") are clozed as parallel `c1` answers so both arms of the decision are drilled together.

This differs from a plain definition/term card (which hides a noun the rest of the sentence defines) because here the hidden token is a verb of causation or a direction, and the surrounding text is the mechanism, not a description. It differs from a pure list card because the items are causally ordered or directional, not interchangeable.

**Canonical syntax:** `{{c1::cause/effect/step}} with directional cues as {{cN::direction::optionA or optionB}}; chain links as shared cN (revealed together) or sequential c1/c2/c3 (interrogated separately)`

**When to use:** Use when the fact IS a relationship  -  an agent acting on a target, a direction of change, or a sequence of steps  -  and the test-worthy point is the causal link or its direction, not a standalone label. Reach for it for pathways, enzyme regulation, drug mechanisms, and pathophysiologic cascades.

**Watch out for:** Don't cloze a direction word without an `::up/down` style cue  -  the grammar of the sentence often gives it away. Avoid clozing so many words in one chain that the sentence collapses into nonsense with no recallable scaffold; keep enough visible context that each blank is answerable. Don't split a tightly paired contrast (downregulates X / upregulates Y) into different groups if they're really one idea.

**Best practices**

- Cloze the verb of causation or the direction (activates/inhibits, up/down, enhances/impairs) when that is the real point of confusion, not just the noun.
- Add a binary or option-list hint (::activated or inhibited, ::enhance/impair, ::increase or decrease) so a directional answer can't be inferred from sentence grammar.
- For an ordered pathway memorized as one unit, give every step the SAME cloze group so the whole sequence is revealed together.
- For a multi-link cascade where each step is independently test-worthy, use sequential groups (c1, c2, c3) so the rest of the chain stays visible as scaffolding.
- Render the chain with explicit arrows (A → B → C) so the causal direction is visually unambiguous before and after revealing.
- Cloze both arms of a branching decision (mild → observe; severe → treat) as parallel answers in one group to drill the contrast together.
- Keep the agent, the action, and the target all present in the sentence; hide only the one element whose recall you are testing.

**Worked examples (171)**

#### 18.1  Simple A→B→C conversion pathway, sequential clozes · biochem (urea cycle)

**Raw `Text` field:**

```
The <i>urea cycle</i> converts {{c1::ammonia}} to {{c1::<b>urea</b>}}&nbsp;which is then excreted in {{c2::urine}}.
```

**Reads as →**

The urea cycle converts 【c1: ammonia】 to 【c1: urea】 which is then excreted in 【c2: urine】.

**`Extra` field →**

Amino acid metabolism produces ammonia which is toxic to the body and must be excreted.

 [image: 6c2f2e257d8d77c6ce3ec33976e12be1.webp]

> **Why it works:** A clean two-link causal chain (ammonia → urea → urine) with the substrate/product pair grouped and the destination its own group, showing the most basic mechanism structure.

---
#### 18.2  Single directional effect verb clozed · physiology (2,3-BPG and O2)

**Raw `Text` field:**

```
<b><i>2,3-BPG</i>&nbsp;</b>causes heme to&nbsp;{{c1::release}} O<sub style="">2</sub>.
```

**Reads as →**

2,3-BPG causes heme to 【release】 O2.

**`Extra` field →**

Creates a right shift just like a low pH would

 [image: 1a6f16a5109071f73225497e04d9a34a.webp]

 
2,3 BPG is an isomer of an intermediate in glycolysis (1,3-BPG) with two phosphate groups (note it's negative and when we exercise, a lot will be produced). So it can only bind to a hemoglobin without any of the four oxygen, it connects to two positive groups (remember 2,3 BPG is negative) and causes a conformational change that, when bound, causes hemoglobin to have a much lower affinity for oxygen.
 
YouTube Link

> **Why it works:** Minimal case: the entire card hides one direction-of-effect word (release), the essence of clozing the causal action.

#### 18.3  Direction-of-effect with enhance/impair cue · pharm (PPIs and fat absorption)

**Raw `Text` field:**

```
<b>Proton pump inhibitors</b> {{c1::enhance::enhance/impair}} fat absorption
```

**Reads as →**

Proton pump inhibitors 【enhance ⟨hint: enhance/impair⟩】 fat absorption

**`Extra` field →**

- Useful in patients taking pancreatic enzyme replacement; exogenously-administered pancreatic lipase is normally inactivated by low pH → PPIs prevent this by reducing gastric acid secretion

- Contrast with impaired absorption of divalent cations (calcium, iron, magnesium) and vitamin B12

> **Why it works:** Demonstrates the directional cue `::enhance/impair` that stops grammar from leaking a binary answer.

#### 18.4  Increase/decrease direction with cue · gen chem (common ion effect)

**Raw `Text` field:**

```
The {{c3::<b>common ion effect</b>}}&nbsp;causes {{c2::solubility}} to {{c1::decrease::increase or decrease}} when {{c2::adding like ions::what happens?}}.
```

**Reads as →**

The 【c3: common ion effect】 causes 【c2: solubility】 to 【c1: decrease ⟨hint: increase or decrease⟩】 when 【c2: adding like ions ⟨hint: what happens?⟩】.

**`Extra` field →**

Imagine trying to dissolve NaCl in 1L of chlorinated water. Consider this an application of Le Chatelier's principle: since there is a bunch of Cl- already, equilibrium will be pushed to the left. NaCl would be much more soluble in distilled water. 

NaCl_((s)) ⇌ Na^(+)_((aq)) + Cl^(-)_((aq))

Q_(sp) = [Na][Cl]

Khan Academy Link

> **Why it works:** Shows the `::increase or decrease` hint applied to a chemistry mechanism, generalizing the directional pattern beyond medicine.

#### 18.29  Condition (low pH) causes molecular state · biochem (amino acid protonation)

**Raw `Text` field:**

```
A {{c2::<u>low</u>}}&nbsp;pH will cause amino acids to be {{c1::fully protonated}}.
```

**Reads as →**

A 【c2: low】 pH will cause amino acids to be 【c1: fully protonated】.

**`Extra` field →**

Effect of pH: 

- The ionization state of an amino acid varies with pH cause each group has its own pka
- Amino acids at physiological pH exist as dipolar ions where the carboxyl group is deprotonated and the amino group is protonated 
- At an acidic pH of ~2 or below, both the amino group (-NH3+) and the carboxyl group are protonated (-COOH)
- As the pH is raised, the carboxylic acid gives up a proton
- The dipolar form persists until the pH approaches 9, when the protonated amino group loses a proton
