#### 18.38  One stimulus, five hemodynamic effects with directions · physiology (obstructive shock)

**Raw `Text` field:**

```
How does <b>obstructive shock</b> affect the following?<br><br><u>CVP</u>: {{c1::increased}}<br><div><u>PCWP</u>: {{c1::<i>decreased</i> in pulmonary causes, <i>increased</i> in cardiac causes::2}}</div><div><u>Cardiac index</u>: {{c1::decreased}}</div><div><u>SVR</u>: {{c1::increased}}</div><div><u>SvO<sub>2</sub></u>: {{c1::decreased}}</div>
```

**Reads as →**

How does obstructive shock affect the following?

CVP: 【c1: increased】
PCWP: 【c1: decreased in pulmonary causes, increased in cardiac causes ⟨hint: 2⟩】
Cardiac index: 【c1: decreased】
SVR: 【c1: increased】
SvO_(2): 【c1: decreased】

**`Extra` field →**

- Pulmonary causes include pulmonary embolism, pulmonary hypertension, and tension pneumothorax

- Cardiac causes include cardiac tamponade, constrictive pericarditis, and restrictive cardiomyopathy

↑ CVP: right sided preload/ central venous pressure increases due to inability to pump fluid out

↓ PCWP in pulm causes: b/c fluid is restricted from reaching the left heart chambers

↑ PCWP in cardio causes: b/c of backup of fluid in the lungs trying to get into the left heart chambers

↓ CI: primary disturbance; the heart can't pump against extra-cardiac blockage
↑ SVR: compensatory activation of the SNS → ↑ SVR to try to increase BP

↓ SvO_(2): decreased perfusion signals tissues to extract more oxygen

 [image: 2eae0f06ea4049483f295e759e3343da.webp]

 [image: 01700cb9d731a0dcdeebe7d7ca512d37.webp]

**`One by one` field →** y

> **Why it works:** A wide causal fan-out: a single condition mapped to five directional outcomes, all in one group, showing how to drill an entire effect-profile.

```

**Reads as →**

#### 18.160  PPV increases intrathoracic pressure then decreases RV preload · physiology

**Raw `Text` field:**

```
<u>Positive pressure mechanical ventilation</u> causes an acute {{c1::increase::increase/decrease}} in <b>intrathoracic</b> <b>pressure</b>,<b> </b>which {{c1::decreases::increases/decreases}} <b>RV preload </b>by compressing the IVC
```

**Reads as →**

Positive pressure mechanical ventilation causes an acute 【c1: increase ⟨hint: increase/decrease⟩】 in intrathoracic pressure, which 【c1: decreases ⟨hint: increases/decreases⟩】 RV preload by compressing the IVC

**`Extra` field →**

- Loss of RV preload can lead to sudden cardiac death
- In the setting of decreased CVP (e.g., hypovolemic shock) → acute loss of RV preload can result in sudden cardiac death

In addition:

- Decreased RV preload & increased intrathoracic pressure (RV afterload) → decreased LV preload
- Decreased MAP (baroreceptor effect) & decreased LV transmural pressure → decreased LV afterload

> **Why it works:** Two opposite directional links in one chain, using increase/decrease cue hints.

## 19. Ordered & Sequential-Step Cards

Some facts are not just lists but *sequences*: synthesis pathways, signaling cascades, anatomic conduction routes, diagnostic algorithms, developmental stages. The teaching goal is twofold  -  recall each member AND preserve the order. The cloze card achieves this by writing the steps in their true order in the stem (as a numbered list `1. … 2. …` or an arrow chain `A → B → C`) and clozing the steps, never reordering them.

There are two clozing modes. **Sequential** gives each step its own cloze number so they reveal one at a time: `{{c1::Engagement}} → {{c2::Descent}} → {{c3::Flexion}}`  -  the reader must produce the next step with all earlier ones still hidden, which drills the order hardest. **Grouped** puts the whole ordered set under one number so all steps test together: `{{c1::Time}} → {{c1::place}} → {{c1::person}}`. Use sequential when each transition is independently testworthy; use grouped when the chain is a single inseparable unit. A common hybrid clozes the *name* of the pathway/syndrome under one number and the ordered steps under another (e.g. `{{c2::Spinal shock}}` describes `{{c1::a}}reflexia → {{c1::hypo}}reflexia → {{c1::hyper}}reflexia`).

Literal syntax: arrow chain  -  `Cochlea → … → inferior colliculus → {{c1::medial geniculate nucleus}} → auditory cortex`; numbered cascade  -  `1. {{c1::↓ Renal perfusion}} → 2. {{c2::↑ RAAS}} → 3. {{c3::Na⁺/H₂O retention}}`. A `::hint` after the answer scopes ambiguity, e.g. `{{c1::3' → 5'::direction}}`. A count hint like `::2` signals how many items the blank hides.

This differs from a plain unordered set/list card (where order is irrelevant and items are interchangeable) precisely because here the *position* is part of the answer  -  keep the steps physically in order in the stem, and never enable list-shuffle on these notes. It differs from cause-and-effect mechanism cards in that the emphasis is the *ordinal chain itself*, though a long mechanism written as A→B→C is really both.

**Canonical syntax:** `Write steps in true order in the stem; cloze each step sequentially ({{c1::A}} → {{c2::B}} → {{c3::C}}) when each transition matters, or grouped under one number ({{c1::A}} → {{c1::B}} → {{c1::C}}) when the chain is one unit.`

**When to use:** Use for any fact where ORDER is part of the answer  -  synthesis/metabolic pathways, signaling and physiologic cascades, anatomic conduction routes, stepwise diagnostic/treatment algorithms, and developmental or staged sequences.

**Watch out for:** Don't reorder steps or enable list-shuffle on ordered notes  -  that destroys the very thing being taught. Don't cram a genuinely ordered cascade under one grouped cloze if each transition is independently testworthy, and don't use separate cloze numbers if the set is truly inseparable.

**Best practices**

- Lay the steps out in their real order in the stem (numbered list or → chain) and keep them there  -  the stem itself encodes the sequence.
- Use sequential cloze numbers (c1→c2→c3) when you want each step recalled with the others hidden; this drills order most aggressively.
- Use one grouped cloze number when the chain is an inseparable unit you always recall together.
- Clozing the pathway/syndrome name under its own number while the ordered steps share another number tests both 'what is this' and 'what are its steps' from one note.
- Leave fixed connective text (arrows, '→', 'followed by', the final node) outside the cloze so the order scaffold stays visible as a cue.
- Add a `::direction` or `::#` style hint when a step's form is ambiguous, and a `::n` count hint when a blank hides multiple items.
- Never turn on list-shuffle for a card whose meaning depends on sequence.

#### 19.3  Fill the missing node in the visual pathway (eye→…→visual cortex) · neuroscience

**Raw `Text` field:**

```
<div>The item missing from the <u>visual pathway</u>:<br></div><br><div>Eye&nbsp;→&nbsp;optic nerves&nbsp;→&nbsp;optic chiasm&nbsp;→&nbsp;optic tracts&nbsp;→&nbsp;{{c1::lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN)}}&nbsp;→&nbsp;visual radiations&nbsp;→&nbsp;visual cortex<br></div>
```

**Reads as →**

Eye → optic nerves → optic chiasm → optic tracts → 【lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN)】 → visual radiations → visual cortex

**`Extra` field →**

[image: 322b9167312771518a899f1453907323.png]
Photo Credit: Miquel Perello Nieto, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
Imagine a beam of light entering the eye and traveling through a series of checkpoints:

- Eye: Light enters the eye and is detected by the retina.
- Optic Nerves: Signals are sent from the retina via the optic nerves.
- Optic Chiasm: Information crosses sides here (from nasal retinas).
- Optic Tracts: Signals travel down the optic tracts.
- LGN: Information is processed and relayed in the thalamus (LGN).
- Visual Radiations: Signals are distributed to the visual cortex.
- Visual Cortex: Final processing for conscious visual perception.
so, Eye detects it → optic nerves carry the signal → optic chiasm for crossing → optic tracts continue → LGN for relay → visual radiations → visual cortex processes the image.

#### 19.5  Spinal shock named (c1) + areflexia→hyporeflexia→hyperreflexia chain (c1) · physiology

**Raw `Text` field:**

```
{{c1::<b>Spinal shock</b>}} describes a change from {{c2::a}}reflexia → {{c2::hypo}}reflexia → {{c2::hyper}}reflexia in patients with <u>spinal cord injuries</u>
```

**Reads as →**

【c1: Spinal shock】 describes a change from 【c2: a】reflexia → 【c2: hypo】reflexia → 【c2: hyper】reflexia in patients with spinal cord injuries

**`Extra` field →**

This is because reflex arcs have become used to a level of tonic stimulation from the brain:

- When they lose tonic stimulation, they try to upregulate more neurotransmitter receptors (areflexia to hyporeflexia) to return to normal

- However, interneurons and lower motor neurons also try to return to normal by nerve sprouting (from axons and somas) to re-establish synapses → two forms of compensation leads to overcompensation

> **Why it works:** Hybrid: clozes the phenomenon name under one number and the ordered progression under another, using shared-stem word-fragment clozing.

RNA → protein = translation: mRNA read in 5′ → 3′ direction

## 20. Classifications & Enumerations

Classifications & Enumerations cards teach the *members of a set*: the subtypes of a parent concept, the categories under a heading, or the named steps in an ordered sequence. The defining move is to **name the parent explicitly in the stem** ("the three layers of the adrenal cortex", "the four phases of mitosis", "types of HPV") and then cloze each member so recall is keyed to that parent.

There are two structural flavors, both shown in the pool. **Grouped recall** puts every member under the *same* cloze index, e.g. `The four phases of Mitosis: {{c1::Prophase}} {{c1::Metaphase}} {{c1::Anaphase}} {{c1::Telophase}}`  -  all four blank together on one card, forcing recall of the whole set at once (note `max_group=4`). **Individuated recall** gives each member its *own* index, e.g. `{{c1::Early primary syphilis}} {{c2::Late untreated syphilis}} {{c3::Prior treated syphilis}}`  -  producing one card per member so each is tested in isolation. Choose grouped when the value is knowing the complete list (you want no member forgotten); choose individuated when each member carries distinct weight or you want spaced, separable testing.

A hint is often attached with the `::` separator. The most useful pattern here is a **count hint** telling the learner how many items to produce, e.g. `{{c1::Hypercoagulable state, embolism, and hemoglobinopathy::3}}` or `{{c1::HPV 6, 11, 16, 18, 31, 33::x6}}`  -  this stops the card from feeling open-ended. A **category hint** like `{{c1::oxidoreductase::type of enzyme}}` signals what *kind* of answer the slot wants. Syntax: `{{c1::member::hint}}`.

This differs from neighboring techniques: a plain definition card clozes one term against its meaning, whereas a classification card's whole point is the *set membership* relation  -  "these N things all belong to parent X." When a single card enumerates several coordinate members, it is this technique; when it pairs one concept with one attribute, it is not.

**Canonical syntax:** `Parent named in stem; members clozed  -  grouped (same index: {{c1::A}} {{c1::B}} {{c1::C}}) or individuated (distinct indices: {{c1::A}} {{c2::B}} {{c3::C}}), optionally with a count or category hint: {{c1::member::hint}}`

**When to use:** Use when the learning objective is the set of subtypes/categories/components/steps under a named parent concept. Pick grouped indices to force recall of the complete list, individuated indices to test each member separately.

**Watch out for:** Don't enumerate a set so long that grouped recall becomes a memory dump with no scaffolding  -  add a count hint (::3, ::x6) or split into individuated cards. Don't leave the parent unnamed in the stem, or the learner can't know which set is being asked for. And don't mix unrelated members under one index just to save cards.

**Best practices**

- State the parent/whole in the stem ('the three layers of...', 'types of...') so the card has a clear retrieval cue.
- Use one shared cloze index across all members when you want the entire set recalled together; use distinct indices when each member deserves its own card.
- Attach a count hint (::3, ::x6) to grouped enumerations so the learner knows how many items to produce and the prompt isn't open-ended.
- Use a category hint (::type of enzyme, ::Hormone) when the slot's answer kind isn't obvious from the stem alone.
- Keep grouped lists short (roughly 3-5 members); split longer or heterogeneous sets into individuated cards.
- Number or order members in the stem when the classification is inherently sequential (mitosis phases, anatomical zones outermost-to-innermost).
- Put the mnemonic, examples, and the per-member details (e.g. what distinguishes each subtype) in the EXTRA field, not the cloze.

**Worked examples (124)**

#### 20.1  Simple count of subunits with # hint · cell signaling

**Raw `Text` field:**

```
<div><b>G proteins</b> have {{c1::three::#}} subunits</div>
```

**Reads as →**

G proteins have 【three ⟨hint: #⟩】 subunits

**`Extra` field →**

alpha, beta, and gamma

> **Why it works:** Cleanest possible classification seed: parent named ('G proteins'), the cardinality clozed with a terse '#' hint, members listed in EXTRA.

#### 20.79  Organophosphate poisoning two-part treatment with drug+target · pharm

**Raw `Text` field:**

```
<u>Treating</u> <b>organophosphate poisoning</b> is two fold: <br><br>- {{c1::<b>Atropine</b>}}, which inhibits all subtypes of {{c1::<b>muscarinic receptors</b>}}<br>- {{c2::<b>Pralidoxime</b>}}, which if given early, regenerates {{c2::<b>acetylcholinesterase</b> (AChE)}}
```

**Reads as →**

Treating organophosphate poisoning is two fold:

- 【c1: Atropine】, which inhibits all subtypes of 【c1: muscarinic receptors】
- 【c2: Pralidoxime】, which if given early, regenerates 【c2: acetylcholinesterase (AChE)】

**`Extra` field →**

- Organophosphates induce cholinergic toxicity

- Treat with atropine first, because pralidoxime can cause transient inhibition of AChE, which will worsen symptoms

| Drug | MOA | Treats | Other |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Pralidoxime | Regenerates AChE | Cholinergic toxicity(e.g., organophosphate / cholinesterase inhibitor toxicity) | |
| Pyridostigmine | AChE inhibitor | Myasthenia gravis | Does not cross BBB |
| Physostigmine | AChE inhibitor | Anticholinergic toxicity(e.g., atropine, Jimson weed) | Crosses BBB |

## 21. Negation & Exception Cards

A negation/exception card tests what is NOT true, the lone exception to a rule, a contraindication, or the least-likely option. The trap these cards defuse is that learners pattern-match the general rule and forget the carve-out. The fix is to make the negation visually unmissable and to put the cloze on the exceptional fact itself, not on a routine item the stem already establishes.

The canonical shape is a stem that states the rule plus an explicit negator (`NOT`, `except`, `cannot`, `never`, `contraindicated`, `does not`) with the exception clozed: `Apolipoprotein E is found on every lipoprotein except {{c1::LDL}}` or `Drug X is contraindicated in {{c1::asthma}}`. Always bold or capitalize the negator in the rendered card (`EXCEPT`, `NOT`, `never`) so the reader cannot misread an exception card as a normal one. For yes/no facts, the cleanest pattern clozes the polarity word with a binary hint: `{{c1::cannot::can/cannot}}` or `{{c1::does NOT::does/does not}}` forces the learner to commit to the direction rather than recall a noun.

Use this technique whenever a fact is memorable precisely because it breaks a pattern: the one drug that is safe, the one tissue spared, the one structure not covered, the test that does not cross-react. Choose between two cloze targets deliberately. Clozing the EXCEPTION (`except {{c1::LDL}}`) tests recall of the carve-out; clozing the POLARITY (`{{c1::cannot::can/cannot}}`) tests whether the learner knows a rule is being violated at all. A paired set (`Candida does {{c1::not}} change pH` / `Gardnerella {{c1::does}} change pH`) drills both sides of a discriminating feature.

This differs from a plain definitional cloze (which hides a positive term in a true statement) and from a compare/contrast card (which juxtaposes two like things). Here the load-bearing element is the negation: remove the `NOT`/`except`/`cannot` and the card becomes false or trivially wrong, so the negator must be preserved in plain text and made loud.

**Canonical syntax:** `Stem with an explicit, emphasized negator (NOT / except / cannot / never / contraindicated) and the exception or polarity clozed: ...except {{c1::exception}} / ...is {{c1::contraindicated}} in ... / ...{{c1::cannot::can/cannot}}...`

**When to use:** Use when a fact is worth knowing because it breaks the general rule: the single exception, a contraindication, the least-likely option, or a counterintuitive negative property. Pick whether to cloze the exception itself or the polarity word depending on which is the real test point.

**Watch out for:** Don't bury the negator in lowercase where the reader skims past it and answers the rule. Don't cloze the negator AND leave no other context, or the card becomes a guessable yes/no; pair it with a binary hint like ::can/cannot. Avoid clozing a routine term so the exception is given away in plain text.

**Best practices**

- Capitalize or bold the negator (EXCEPT, NOT, never, cannot) in the rendered card so an exception card is never misread as a normal one.
- Decide deliberately whether to cloze the exception (the carve-out fact) or the polarity word (does/does not), based on which is the actual test point.
- For yes/no polarity, cloze the direction word with a binary hint: {{c1::cannot::can/cannot}} or {{c1::does NOT::does/does not}}.
- Keep the general rule visible in plain text so the contrast that makes the exception notable is preserved.
- Make paired cards for discriminating features (one entity does X, the other does NOT) to drill both directions.
- Put the 'why' (mechanism behind the exception or contraindication) in the EXTRA field, not the stem.
- Anchor multi-item exclusion lists with a count hint (::2) so the learner recalls the full set.

**Worked examples (43)**

#### 21.1  polarity cloze with binary hint (can/cannot) · pharmacology

**Raw `Text` field:**

```
<b>Vancomycin</b> {{c1::can::can/cannot}} penetrate the CNS
```

**Reads as →**

Vancomycin 【can ⟨hint: can/cannot⟩】 penetrate the CNS

**`Extra` field →**

Used in the empiric treatment of meningitis with ceftriaxone

> **Why it works:** Cleanest template for a yes/no fact: the direction word itself is clozed with a ::can/cannot hint, forcing commitment to polarity.

## 22. Clinical Vignettes

A clinical vignette card builds a short, self-contained scenario (the stem) and then clozes the single highest-yield conclusion the scenario points to  -  most often a diagnosis, but also the causal mechanism, the next diagnostic step, or the definitive treatment. The whole point is that the learner reads a realistic patient story and must *commit to one answer*, the way they would on an exam or at the bedside. The cloze goes on the conclusion, never on the clinical clues that make the scenario solvable.

The simplest form is a one-blank stem: `A young patient presents with progressive lower-limb weakness, scoliosis, high plantar arches, decreased vibratory/position sense, and cervical cord atrophy on MRI. What is the best diagnostic test? {{c1::Genetic testing (frataxin gene)}}`  -  every detail in the stem is a discriminating feature of Friedreich ataxia, and exactly one blank holds the payoff. You can cloze a *diagnosis* (`...bizarre behavior, impaired attention, CD4 < 200, diffuse white-matter signal → {{c1::HIV-associated neurocognitive disorder}}`), a *mechanism* (`hallucinations in a febrile toddler given OTC cough/cold meds → {{c1::antihistamine/anticholinergic side effect}}`), or a *next step / pathway*. Use a hint when the answer category needs signposting: `{{c1::hydrocephalus::diagnosis}}` and `{{c1::ultrasound / MRI::next step}}` let one stem ask for both the label and the action without ambiguity.

More sophisticated variants chain the cloze: a stem can ask 'what would happen if...' and cloze the mechanistic cascade (`positive-pressure ventilation would {{c1::increase::increase / decrease}} intrathoracic air → {{c1::exacerbate}} the tension pneumothorax → {{c1::cardiovascular collapse}}`), or present several mini-vignettes that must be discriminated against each other (`Stiffness > pain, ↑ESR, normal CK → {{c1::Polymyalgia rheumatica}}` vs. `proximal weakness, ↑ESR, ↑CK → {{c1::Polymyositis}}`). The contrast format is powerful because the differentiating lab/feature is left visible and only the verdict is hidden, forcing pattern-to-diagnosis mapping.

This technique differs from a plain definition or list card: a definition card states a fact and blanks a term, while a vignette *makes the learner do diagnostic reasoning* from clues to conclusion. It also differs from mnemonic-feature cards (which blank every item of a CRASH/MUDPILES list); a vignette deliberately blanks only the endpoint so the cue stays rich and the recall stays single-answer.

**Canonical syntax:** `Realistic scenario stem with discriminating clues left visible, then one {{c1::diagnosis/mechanism/next step}} (optionally {{c1::answer::category-hint}}) on the conclusion`

**When to use:** Use when you want to drill diagnostic or clinical-reasoning pattern recognition  -  mapping a constellation of signs, symptoms, labs, or imaging to the correct diagnosis, underlying mechanism, or next management step. Ideal for board-style 'most likely diagnosis / best next test' material.

**Watch out for:** Don't scatter blanks across the clues  -  clozing the discriminating findings destroys the cue and turns the card into trivia. Keep the stem self-contained (no reliance on a missing image) and cloze exactly one conclusion (or one tight chain) so there is a single defensible answer.

**Best practices**

- Put the cloze on the endpoint (diagnosis, mechanism, or next step), and leave every discriminating clue in the stem visible.
- Make the stem self-contained: include the labs/imaging/history needed to reach one answer without seeing a picture.
- Add a category hint like ::diagnosis or ::next step when one stem asks for more than one type of answer, so each blank is unambiguous.
- Pack the stem with the high-yield discriminators that distinguish this entity from its mimics (e.g., normal CK vs. ↑CK), not generic filler.
- For 'what happens if...' cards, cloze the causal chain in order so the learner reconstructs the mechanism step by step.
- Use side-by-side mini-vignettes when teaching a differential: keep the distinguishing feature shown and cloze only the verdict for each.
- Keep the answer specific and the only correct one  -  avoid stems that could plausibly yield several diagnoses.

**Worked examples (43)**

#### 22.1  One-blank diagnostic-test stem (Friedreich ataxia clues) · neurology

**Raw `Text` field:**

```
A young patient presents with <b>progressive</b> weakness in the lower limbs. She has a history of <u>scoliosis</u> and <u>high plantar arches</u>. <b>Strength is 2/5 in the lower limbs</b> and 5/5 in the upper limbs. <b>Decreased vibratory and position sense</b> is noted in the lower extremities. MRI shows cervical spinal cord atrophy.<br><br><div>What is the best diagnostic test? </div><br><div>{{c1::Genetic testing (<i>frataxin gene</i>)}}</div>
```

**Reads as →**

A young patient presents with progressive weakness in the lower limbs. She has a history of scoliosis and high plantar arches. Strength is 2/5 in the lower limbs and 5/5 in the upper limbs. Decreased vibratory and position sense is noted in the lower extremities. MRI shows cervical spinal cord atrophy.

What is the best diagnostic test?

【Genetic testing (frataxin gene)】

**`Extra` field →**

The patient most likely has Friedreich ataxia

 [image: b9c41ed420805cfe1d800bd2c9b3a686.webp]

> **Why it works:** Cleanest template: a clue-rich stem with exactly one blank on the 'best diagnostic test', showing how a vignette should read.

#### 22.2  Single-cloze mechanism for a pediatric presentation (OTC cough/cold) · pharmacology/toxicology

**Raw `Text` field:**

```
What is the <i>most likely explanation</i> for <b>hallucinations</b> in a young boy with <u>fever, runny nose, and a cough</u> who appears to be <b>talking to someone in the room</b> and says <b>he can see his old cat</b>? The parents have tried OTC cough and cold medications for the past 36 hours. Labs are significant for fever of 101° F<br><br><div>{{c1::Medication side effect due to antihistamines}}</div>
```

**Reads as →**

What is the most likely explanation for hallucinations in a young boy with fever, runny nose, and a cough who appears to be talking to someone in the room and says he can see his old cat? The parents have tried OTC cough and cold medications for the past 36 hours. Labs are significant for fever of 101° F

【Medication side effect due to antihistamines】

**`Extra` field →**

- Most OTC preparations contain antihistamines, but also have anticholinergic properties that can cause confusion and hallucinations

- Cough suppressant dextromethorphan can also cause dissociative symptoms and hallucinations

> **Why it works:** Demonstrates clozing the *mechanism/explanation* rather than a diagnosis, off a vivid bedside scenario.

**Raw `Text` field:**

```
<b>Determine the diagnosis</b> for the three vignettes below (<u>fibromyalgia</u> OR <u>polymyositis</u> OR <u>polymyalgia rheumatica</u>)<br><br><div>

<ul class="shuffle" style="padding-left: 0 !important; width: 90% !important; max-width: 90% !important;">
  <li style="text-align: center; list-style-type: none;"><b>Stiffness</b> &gt; pain in proximal muscles with <u>elevated ESR and normal creatine kinase</u>: {{c1::Polymyalgia rheumatica}}</li></ul></div><br><div>

#### 22.7  'What would happen if...' clozed mechanistic cascade · emergency/critical care

**Raw `Text` field:**

```
What would occur if a patient with a tension pneumothorax was intubated <i>before</i> <u>chest decompression</u> (needle or tube thoracostomy)?<br><br>The positive-pressure ventilation would {{c1::increase::increase / decrease}} accumulated air in the {{c1::intrathoracic}} space which would {{c1::exacerbate::relieve / exacerbate}} the tension pneumothorax leading to {{c1::cardiovascular collapse}}
```

**Reads as →**

What would occur if a patient with a tension pneumothorax was intubated before chest decompression (needle or tube thoracostomy)?

The positive-pressure ventilation would 【c1: increase ⟨hint: increase / decrease⟩】 accumulated air in the 【c1: intrathoracic】 space which would 【c1: exacerbate ⟨hint: relieve / exacerbate⟩】 the tension pneumothorax leading to 【c1: cardiovascular collapse】

**`Extra` field →**

- Important exception to the typical order of establishing the airway first

- If a patient with a tension pneumothorax requires mechanical ventilation, immediate tube thoracostomy should be performed first

- Needle thoracostomy is a temporizing measure. Once the patient is out of immediate danger, a thoracostomy tube or catheter should be placed

- If immediately available and appropriate for the clinical situation, a thoracostomy tube or catheter is an alternative for initial decompression

**`One by one` field →** y

> **Why it works:** Advanced form: the cloze chain reconstructs a step-by-step pathophysiologic consequence rather than a single label.

#### 22.13  Survival-improving therapies for a named condition · cardiology/pharm

**Raw `Text` field:**

```
<div>Medications shown to <u>improve long-term survival</u> in patients with <b>LV systolic dysfunction</b> include:</div><div><br><div>1. {{c1::<b>β</b><b>-blockers</b>}}</div><div>2. {{c1::<b>ACEIs </b>(or ARBs)}}</div><div>3. {{c1::<b>Sacubitril-valsartan </b>(ARNIs)}}</div><div>4. {{c1::<b>Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists </b>(MRAs)}} </div><div>5. {{c1::<b>SGLT-2 inhibitors</b>}}</div><div>6. {{c1::<b>Hydralazine</b>}} with {{c1::<b>isosorbide dinitrate</b>}} in African American patients<br></div></div>
```

**Reads as →**

Medications shown to improve long-term survival in patients with LV systolic dysfunction include:

1. 【c1: β-blockers】
2. 【c1: ACEIs (or ARBs)】
3. 【c1: Sacubitril-valsartan (ARNIs)】
4. 【c1: Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (MRAs)】
5. 【c1: SGLT-2 inhibitors】
6. 【c1: Hydralazine】 with 【c1: isosorbide dinitrate】 in African American patients

**`Extra` field →**

- Beta-blockers, RAAS inhibitors (ACEIs/ARBs/ARNIs), SGLT-2 inhibitors, and MRAs are part of Guideline-Directed Medical Therapy (GDMT) for heart failure (improve both survival and hospitalization rates)

- SGLT-2 inhibitors decrease risk of cardiovascular death or hospitalization for heart failure, regardless of the presence or absence of diabetes (EMPEROR-Reduced trial)

 - Diuretics provide symptomatic relief for volume overload but no mortality benefit

 - Digoxin reduces hospitalizations but offers no mortality benefit

#### 22.25  Mitosis vs meiosis contrast with category hints · cell biology

**Raw `Text` field:**

```
Differences in <b>mitosis</b> vs <b>meiosis</b><br><br>- <b>Meiosis</b> results in {{c1::4::#}} daughter cells, while <b>mitosis</b> results in {{c1::2::#}} daughter cells<br>- <b>Meiosis</b> results in {{c1::haploid::haploid/diploid}} cells, while <b>mitosis</b> results in {{c1::diploid::haploid/diploid}} cells<br>- <b>Meiosis</b> occurs to form {{c1::gametes}}, while <b>mitosis</b> is for {{c1::growth/repair}}<br>- <b>Meiosis</b> results in cells that are {{c1::different::identical/different}} from parent cell, while <b>mitosis</b> results in cells that are {{c1::identical::identical/different}} to parent cell
```

**Reads as →**

Differences in mitosis vs meiosis

- Meiosis results in 【c1: 4 ⟨hint: #⟩】 daughter cells, while mitosis results in 【c1: 2 ⟨hint: #⟩】 daughter cells
- Meiosis results in 【c1: haploid ⟨hint: haploid/diploid⟩】 cells, while mitosis results in 【c1: diploid ⟨hint: haploid/diploid⟩】 cells
- Meiosis occurs to form 【c1: gametes】, while mitosis is for 【c1: growth/repair】
- Meiosis results in cells that are 【c1: different ⟨hint: identical/different⟩】 from parent cell, while mitosis results in cells that are 【c1: identical ⟨hint: identical/different⟩】 to parent cell

**`Extra` field →**

Meiosis occurs in gonadal cells to produce haploid sperm and egg cells that each contain 23 chromosomes and combine to form a diploid zygote. 

Oogenesis in females begins in the female embryo. Oocytes are frozen in metaphase II until fertilization.

Spermatogenesis in males does not begin until puberty.

#### 22.30  Stepwise REDOX balancing in acidic solution · chemistry

**Raw `Text` field:**

```
<div>\(Cr_2O^{2-}_7(aq)+C_2O^{2-}_4(aq)\rightarrow Cr^{3+}(aq)+CO_2(g)\)</div><br><div>Balance the above REDOX reaction in an <i>acidic</i> solution:<br></div><br><br><div><b>Step 1:</b>&nbsp;{{c1::Split into half-reactions and balance all atoms except H and O<br>\({{c1::C_2O^{-2}_{4}(aq)\rightarrow2CO_2(g)}}\)<br>\(Cr_2O^{-2}_{7}(aq)\rightarrow2Cr^{3+}(aq)\)}}</div><br><b>Step 2:</b>&nbsp;{{c1::Balance O atoms by adding water<br>\({{c1::C_2O^{-2}_{4}(aq)\rightarrow2CO_2(g)}}\)&nbsp;(already balanced)<br>\(Cr_2O^{-2}_{7}(aq)\rightarrow2Cr^{3+}(aq)+7H_2O(l)\)}}<br><br><b>Step 3:</b>&nbsp;{{c1::Balance H atoms by adding H<sup>+</sup><br>\(C_2O^{-2}_{4}(aq)\rightarrow2CO_2(g)\)&nbsp;(already balanced)<br>\(Cr_2O^{-2}_{7}(aq)+14H^+(aq)\rightarrow2Cr^{3+}(aq)+7H_2O(l)\)}}<br><br><b>Step 4:</b>&nbsp;{{c1::Balance by adding electrons<br>\(C_2O^{-2}_{4}(aq)\rightarrow2CO_2(g)+2e^-\)<br>\(Cr_2O^{-2}_{7}(aq)+14H^+(aq)+6e^-\rightarrow2Cr^{3+}(aq)+7H_2O(l)\)}}<br><br><b>Step 5:</b>&nbsp;{{c1::Make the numbers of electrons the same by multiplication<br>\(3C_2O^{-2}_{4}(aq)\rightarrow6CO_2(g)+6e^-\)<br>\(Cr_2O^{-2}_{7}(aq)+14H^+(aq)+6e^-\rightarrow2Cr^{3+}(aq)+7H_2O(l)\)}}<br><br><div><b>Step 6:</b>&nbsp;{{c1::Sum the equations<br>\(3C_2O^{-2}_{4}(aq)+Cr_2O^{-2}_{7}(aq)+14H^+(aq)\rightarrow6CO_2(g)+2Cr^{3+}(aq)+7H_2O(l)\)}}</div><br>
```

**Reads as →**

\(Cr_2O^{2-}_7(aq)+C_2O^{2-}_4(aq)\rightarrow Cr^{3+}(aq)+CO_2(g)\)

Balance the above REDOX reaction in an acidic solution:

Step 1: 【c1: Split into half-reactions and balance all atoms except H and O \({{c1 ⟨hint: C_2O^{-2}_{4}(aq)\rightarrow2CO_2(g)⟩】\)
\(Cr_2O^{-2}_{7}(aq)\rightarrow2Cr^{3+}(aq)\)}}

Step 2: 【c1: Balance O atoms by adding water \({{c1 ⟨hint: C_2O^{-2}_{4}(aq)\rightarrow2CO_2(g)⟩】\) (already balanced)
\(Cr_2O^{-2}_{7}(aq)\rightarrow2Cr^{3+}(aq)+7H_2O(l)\)}}

Step 3: 【c1: Balance H atoms by adding H^(+) \(C_2O^{-2}_{4}(aq)\rightarrow2CO_2(g)\) (already balanced) \(Cr_2O^{-2}_{7}(aq)+14H^+(aq)\rightarrow2Cr^{3+}(aq)+7H_2O(l)\)】

Step 4: 【c1: Balance by adding electrons \(C_2O^{-2}_{4}(aq)\rightarrow2CO_2(g)+2e^-\) \(Cr_2O^{-2}_{7}(aq)+14H^+(aq)+6e^-\rightarrow2Cr^{3+}(aq)+7H_2O(l)\)】

Step 5: 【c1: Make the numbers of electrons the same by multiplication \(3C_2O^{-2}_{4}(aq)\rightarrow6CO_2(g)+6e^-\) \(Cr_2O^{-2}_{7}(aq)+14H^+(aq)+6e^-\rightarrow2Cr^{3+}(aq)+7H_2O(l)\)】

Step 6: 【c1: Sum the equations \(3C_2O^{-2}_{4}(aq)+Cr_2O^{-2}_{7}(aq)+14H^+(aq)\rightarrow6CO_2(g)+2Cr^{3+}(aq)+7H_2O(l)\)】

#### 22.31  Stepwise REDOX balancing in basic solution · chemistry

**Raw `Text` field:**

```
<div>\(Cr_2O^{2-}_7(aq)+C_2O^{2-}_4\rightarrow Cr^{3+}(aq)+CO_2(g)\)</div><div>Balance the above REDOX reaction in a&nbsp;<u>basic</u>&nbsp;solution:</div><br><div><b>Step 1:</b> {{c1::Follow the steps for an acidic solution}}</div><br><b>Step 2:</b> {{c1::Add OH equal to the number of H<sup>+</sup>&nbsp;on both sides of the equation<br>\(3C_2O^{-2}_{4}(aq)+Cr_2O^{-2}_{7}(aq)+14H^+(aq)+14OH^-(aq)\rightarrow6CO_2(g)+2Cr^{3+}(aq)+7H_2O(l)+14OH^-(aq)\)}}<br><br><b>Step 3:</b> {{c1::Combine to form H<sub>2</sub>O<br>\(3C_2O^{-2}_{4}(aq)+Cr_2O^{-2}_{7}(aq)+14H_20(aq)\rightarrow6CO_2(g)+2Cr^{3+}(aq)+7H_2O(l)+14OH^-(aq)\)}}<br><br><b>Step 4:</b> {{c1::Cancel out equal amount of water from each side<br>\(3C_2O^{-2}_{4}(aq)+Cr_2O^{-2}_{7}(aq)+7H_20(aq)\rightarrow6CO_2(g)+2Cr^{3+}(aq)+14OH^-(aq)\)}}
```

**Reads as →**

\(Cr_2O^{2-}_7(aq)+C_2O^{2-}_4\rightarrow Cr^{3+}(aq)+CO_2(g)\)
Balance the above REDOX reaction in a basic solution:

Step 1: 【c1: Follow the steps for an acidic solution】

Step 2: 【c1: Add OH equal to the number of H^(+) on both sides of the equation \(3C_2O^{-2}_{4}(aq)+Cr_2O^{-2}_{7}(aq)+14H^+(aq)+14OH^-(aq)\rightarrow6CO_2(g)+2Cr^{3+}(aq)+7H_2O(l)+14OH^-(aq)\)】

Step 3: 【c1: Combine to form H_(2)O \(3C_2O^{-2}_{4}(aq)+Cr_2O^{-2}_{7}(aq)+14H_20(aq)\rightarrow6CO_2(g)+2Cr^{3+}(aq)+7H_2O(l)+14OH^-(aq)\)】

Step 4: 【c1: Cancel out equal amount of water from each side \(3C_2O^{-2}_{4}(aq)+Cr_2O^{-2}_{7}(aq)+7H_20(aq)\rightarrow6CO_2(g)+2Cr^{3+}(aq)+14OH^-(aq)\)】

# Part VI - Advanced AnKing Patterns

_Note-type features beyond plain cloze that power high-yield list recall._


## 23. One-by-One Reveal Lists

A One-by-One Reveal List is the AnKing list-recall pattern: you write a vertical list (steps, members of a set, an ordered pathway, a mnemonic's expansion) and wrap EACH item in the SAME cloze number, almost always `c1`. Because every item shares one cloze index, the card has a single card-side, but AnKing's 'One by one' field then reveals the hidden items sequentially as you click, so you must recall item 1, reveal it, recall item 2, reveal it, and so on, instead of seeing the whole answer at once.

The core syntax is just repeated same-index clozes down a list: `- {{c1::Item A}}` / `- {{c1::Item B}}` / `- {{c1::Item C}}`. You may add a per-item hint after a second colon, and the hint is what makes these cards excellent: for an unordered set use a first-letter cue `{{c1::Conscientiousness::C}}` (so a mnemonic like OCEAN drives recall), and for a direction-of-change item use a symbol legend `{{c1::increased::↑↓↔}}`. A literal tiny example: `{{c1::answer::hint}}`.

Reach for this pattern whenever the fact is fundamentally a LIST you want to recall completely and (often) in order: enzyme/anatomy pathways shown with arrows, the steps of a synthesis, the layers of an organ, the components of an acronym, or a panel of lab values that all shift together. The shared `c1` is deliberate  -  it keeps the whole list as one note while still forcing full recall.

Contrast with neighbors: a grouped cloze that hides several phrases under one `c1` blanks them all simultaneously and is for tightly-bound phrases within a sentence, not an enumerable list. Multi-cloze cards (`c1`, `c2`, `c3`) deliberately make SEPARATE cards so each item is tested in isolation  -  use that when items are independent and you do NOT want to recall them together. One-by-one sits between: one card, but complete list recall.

**Canonical syntax:** Same cloze index on every list item: `- {{c1::item1}}` / `- {{c1::item2}}` / `- {{c1::item3::hint}}` (optionally with first-letter or symbol hints).

**When to use:** Use when the fact is an enumerable list, ordered pathway, set of components, or acronym expansion that you want to recall in full (and often in sequence) rather than as isolated facts. Add a hint to each item when a mnemonic letter or a direction-of-change legend helps cue the recall.

**Watch out for:** Do not split list items across different cloze numbers (c1/c2/c3) unless you intentionally want separate cards  -  that breaks the single one-by-one reveal. Avoid putting so many items in one list that the card becomes unmemorable, and don't use this for a single bound phrase (that is a plain or grouped cloze, not a list).

**Best practices**

- Wrap every list item in the SAME cloze index (almost always c1) so the note reveals item by item as one card.
- Preserve order with numbers or arrows when sequence matters (pathways, synthesis steps, taxonomic ranks) and state the direction (broadest→most specific).
- For acronym/mnemonic lists, add a first-letter hint per item, e.g. {{c1::Openness::O}}, so the mnemonic actually drives recall.
- For panels of values that move together, give each a legend hint like {{c1::increased::↑↓↔}} so the card tests the direction, not the wording.
- Keep each item to a short, self-contained phrase; put elaboration and images in the EXTRA field, not in the cloze.
- Name the set in the stem ("The adrenal cortex has three layers", "Monocular cues include") so the learner knows how many items to produce.
- Keep list length reasonable; very long lists recall better with per-item first-letter hints than bare blanks.

**Worked examples (83)**

```

**Reads as →**

What changes occur during the process of spermiogenesis?

 - Loss of 【c1: cytoplasmic contents】
 - Gain of a(n) 【c1: acrosomal】 cap
 - Development of a(n) 【c1: flagellum】

#### 23.13  Arrow pathway anchored to a fixed start · secretory protein trafficking (cell bio)

**Raw `Text` field:**

```
The translation and processing of <b>secretory proteins</b> starts in the cytosol and then proceeds as follows:<br><br>cytosol&nbsp;→ {{c1::rough endoplasmic reticulum}} → {{c1::golgi apparatus}} → {{c1::secretory vesicles}} → {{c1::plasma membrane}}
```

**Reads as →**

The translation and processing of secretory proteins starts in the cytosol and then proceeds as follows:

cytosol → 【c1: rough endoplasmic reticulum】 → 【c1: golgi apparatus】 → 【c1: secretory vesicles】 → 【c1: plasma membrane】

**`Extra` field →**

- Translation of mRNA to proteins begins in the cytosol. From there, proteins meant for cellular use travel to their intracellular destination. 
- However, proteins intended for the secretory pathway have N-terminal signal sequences that causes them to be transferred to the rough endoplasmic reticulum (RER)
- In the RER, post-translational modifications such as glycosylation, disulfide bond formation, phosphorylation, and protein cleavage can occur. 
- The RER then packages proteins into vesicles and sends them to the golgi aparatus for further processing (retrograde processing)
- Finally, the golgi apparatus packages proteins into secretory vesicles which fuse with the plasma membrane and releases the contents outside of the cell

 [image: c450cdedddc0f20c8a9b31c1cebea9c6.webp]

Golgi apparatus: general structure and role in packaging and secretion - Jack Westin

**`One by one` field →** Y

> **Why it works:** Shows leaving the starting node (cytosol) unclozed as a given, so only the recalled steps are hidden.

#### 23.16  3 findings with arrow-legend hints · athlete's heart

**Raw `Text` field:**

```
<b>Athlete's heart</b> results from intensive <u>endurance training</u> and is characterized by:<br><br>- {{c1::↑::↑↓↔}} <b>LV cavity size</b><br>- Slightly {{c1::↑::↑↓↔}} <b>LV wall thickness</b><br>- {{c1::<u>Normal</u>::↑↓↔}} <b>LA size</b>
```

**Reads as →**

Athlete's heart results from intensive endurance training and is characterized by:

- 【c1: ↑ ⟨hint: ↑↓↔⟩】 LV cavity size
- Slightly 【c1: ↑ ⟨hint: ↑↓↔⟩】 LV wall thickness
- 【c1: Normal ⟨hint: ↑↓↔⟩】 LA size

**`Extra` field →**

Other characteristic findings
- ↑ RV cavity size
- ↑ stroke volume with unchanged LVEF (can cause pulmonic valve flow murmur)
- Sinus bradycardia at rest, often with low-grade AV block

- Distinguish from hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM), which is characterized by ↓ LV cavity size, asymmetric LV wall thickening, and ↑ LA size

 [image: ef0d1df6312fbad6aa48ddef52430665.webp]

**`One by one` field →** y

> **Why it works:** Each item is a direction-of-change clozed against a ↑↓↔ legend hint, testing the trend rather than wording.

#### 23.17  5-value hemodynamic panel with a count hint · obstructive shock

**Raw `Text` field:**

```
How does <b>obstructive shock</b> affect the following?<br><br><u>CVP</u>: {{c1::increased}}<br><div><u>PCWP</u>: {{c1::<i>decreased</i> in pulmonary causes, <i>increased</i> in cardiac causes::2}}</div><div><u>Cardiac index</u>: {{c1::decreased}}</div><div><u>SVR</u>: {{c1::increased}}</div><div><u>SvO<sub>2</sub></u>: {{c1::decreased}}</div>
```

**Reads as →**

How does obstructive shock affect the following?

CVP: 【c1: increased】
PCWP: 【c1: decreased in pulmonary causes, increased in cardiac causes ⟨hint: 2⟩】
Cardiac index: 【c1: decreased】
SVR: 【c1: increased】
SvO_(2): 【c1: decreased】

**`Extra` field →**

- Pulmonary causes include pulmonary embolism, pulmonary hypertension, and tension pneumothorax

- Cardiac causes include cardiac tamponade, constrictive pericarditis, and restrictive cardiomyopathy

↑ CVP: right sided preload/ central venous pressure increases due to inability to pump fluid out

↓ PCWP in pulm causes: b/c fluid is restricted from reaching the left heart chambers

↑ PCWP in cardio causes: b/c of backup of fluid in the lungs trying to get into the left heart chambers

↓ CI: primary disturbance; the heart can't pump against extra-cardiac blockage
↑ SVR: compensatory activation of the SNS → ↑ SVR to try to increase BP

↓ SvO_(2): decreased perfusion signals tissues to extract more oxygen

 [image: 2eae0f06ea4049483f295e759e3343da.webp]

 [image: 01700cb9d731a0dcdeebe7d7ca512d37.webp]

**`One by one` field →** y

> **Why it works:** Mixes simple direction clozes with one multi-part item that uses a count hint to signal two expected sub-answers.

#### 23.25  Treatment list with category hints · thyroid storm 4 P's

**Raw `Text` field:**

```
<div>What are the "<b>4 P's</b>" used to treat <b>thyroid storm</b>?</div><br><div> 1. {{c1::<b>P</b>ropranolol::β-blocker}}</div><div> 2. {{c1::<b>P</b>ropylthiouracil (<b>P</b>TU)::Antithyroid agent}} </div><div> 3. {{c1::<b>P</b>rednisolone::Corticosteroid}}</div><div> 4. {{c1::<b>P</b>otassium iodide::Lugol iodine}}</div>
```

**Reads as →**

What are the "4 P's" used to treat thyroid storm?

 1. 【c1: Propranolol ⟨hint: β-blocker⟩】
 2. 【c1: Propylthiouracil (PTU) ⟨hint: Antithyroid agent⟩】
 3. 【c1: Prednisolone ⟨hint: Corticosteroid⟩】
 4. 【c1: Potassium iodide ⟨hint: Lugol iodine⟩】

**`Extra` field →**

Propranolol - blocks sympathetic effects and peripheral conversion of T_(4) to T_(3) (inhibits 5' deiodinase)

PTU - blocks thyroid hormone synthesis and ↓ peripheral conversion of T_(4 )to T_(3)

Prednisolone - inhibits peripheral conversion of T_(4) to T_(3) (inhibits 5' deiodinase) and prevents exophthalmopathy

Potassium iodide - inhibits proteolytic cleavage of T_(3) and T_(4) from thyroglobulin → inhibits thyroid hormone release (Wolff-Chaikoff effect)

 [image: 9c1926278bc86e92b4817ce55fab7c5b.png]

**`One by one` field →** y

> **Why it works:** Each drug is hinted by its drug-class rather than a first letter, showing hints can be semantic cues, not just mnemonics.

#### 23.38  4 phases written as an inline comma list · bacterial growth curve

**Raw `Text` field:**

```
Bacteria are said to grow in a series of <u>four different phases</u>: {{c1::<b>lag</b><b>&nbsp;phase</b>}}<b>,&nbsp;</b>{{c1::<b>exponential phase</b>}}<b>,&nbsp;</b>{{c1::<b>stationary phase</b>}}<b>, </b>and<b>&nbsp;</b>{{c1::<b>death phase</b>}}.
```

**Reads as →**

Bacteria are said to grow in a series of four different phases: 【c1: lag phase】, 【c1: exponential phase】, 【c1: stationary phase】, and 【c1: death phase】.

**`Extra` field →**

- Bacterial growth: the division of one bacterium into two daughter cells in a process called binary fission
- Lag phase: the period of bacterial growth in which bacteria adapt themselves to growth conditions; the individual bacteria are maturing and not yet able to divide
- Logarithmic: forming a straight line when plotted on a logarithmic scale; exponential
- Binary fission: the process whereby a cell divides asexually to produce two daughter cells
- Exponential phase: is a period characterized by cell doubling in a population
- Stationary phase: the size of a population of bacteria remains constant, even though some cells continue to divide and others begin to die
- Death phase: period that begins when cells in culture exhaust their nutrient supply and begin to die

 [image: 0d5383ee132584fccf46981e99778979.webp]
Photo Credit: Original by Gonn, translated by Alex Nico, CC BY-SA 4.0, Via Wikimedia Commons Original by Gonn, translated by Alex Nico, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

The growth of a bacterial population occurs when bacteria undergo binary fission to reproduce. The rate at which this occurs can be demonstrated by plotting a typical growth curve that includes the following phases: lag, exponential growth, stationary, and death. This growth curve can change when bacteria are incubated with an antibiotic (ie, a substance that inhibits growth).

**`One by one` field →** Y

> **Why it works:** Shows the one-by-one set can live inline in a sentence (comma-separated) rather than as bulleted lines.

**`Extra` field →**

- Non-osmotic release of ADH due to AT2, hypovolemia and hypotension. [goal is to replete volume]
- Renin/aldosterone due to decreased renal perfusion → RAAS

- Results in hypovolemic hyponatremia due to retention of a relative excess of total body water

- Treat hypovolemic hyponatremia with normal saline to treat hyponatremia, restore euvolemia → shut-off non-osmotic ADH release

**Reads as →**

Pulmonary artery pressure: 【c1: increased】

**`Extra` field →**

- Decreased LA pressure (measured as PCWP) suggests an intrinsic pulmonary process → obstructive shock (↓ blood to LA)

- An increased PCWP suggests left-sided heart failure leading to right-sided heart failure

- Normal PCWP reflects normal left ventricular function, suggesting that the elevated pulmonary pressures seen are due to an intrinsic pulmonary process

Complications of acute kidney injury include 【c1: hypervolemia ⟨hint: H_(2)O⟩】, 【c1: hyperkalemia ⟨hint: K^(+)⟩】, 【c1: metabolic acidosis ⟨hint: HCO_(3)^(-)⟩】, 【c1: uremia ⟨hint: BUN⟩】, and infection

**`Extra` field →**

- Cannot pee out water or urea
- Less Na^(+) in, less H^(+)/K^(+) out

#### 23.81  Acute cholangitis treatment as an ordered arrow sequence · surgery

**Raw `Text` field:**

```
What is the <i>treatment</i> of <b>acute cholangitis</b>?<br><br><div>{{c1::Stabilize patient as needed (e.g., IV fluids)}} → {{c1::start empiric abx (pip-tazo or ceft + metro)}} → {{c1::ERCP guided biliary drainage}} → {{c1::interval cholecystectomy}}</div>
```

**Reads as →**

What is the treatment of acute cholangitis?

【c1: Stabilize patient as needed (e.g., IV fluids)】 → 【c1: start empiric abx (pip-tazo or ceft + metro)】 → 【c1: ERCP guided biliary drainage】 → 【c1: interval cholecystectomy】

**`Extra` field →**

- Coverage for common enteric pathogens and potential anaerobes

- Common first-line antibiotic is piperacillin-tazobactam; may also use ceftriaxone (or ciprofloxacin) with metronidazole

- Choice of empiric antibiotic is based on the severity of the infection (mild, moderate, or severe) and whether the infection is community-acquired or hospital-acquired

**`One by one` field →** y

> **Why it works:** Whole management pathway clozed step-by-step so each next-step reveals in order.

```

**Reads as →**

How will lowering the cutoff value for the fasting glucose level that indicates diabetes affect the following:

Sensitivity: 【c1: increase】
Specificity: 【c1: decrease】
PPV: 【c1: decrease】
NPV: 【c1: increase】

**`Extra` field →**

Raise cutoff point: Will increase things with "p" in the word (p for +, like raising) - specificity and PPV increase, and the opposite is the case for sensitivity/NPV. Everything is reversed for lowering the cutoff point

- The 3 topical drugs are typically given in succession with a minute in-between each application
